groups.label: Siege of Quebec
groups.definition: Reports of the American siege of Quebec in the 1776 papers: Montgomery's letter calling on Carleton to surrender (December 1775), the account of the failed assault of 31 December, and a camp letter of 6 April 1776. Contains those three groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: Montgomery's letter to Carleton
groups.definition: Printings of General Montgomery's letter to Governor Carleton from before Quebec, dated December 1775, calling on him to surrender the town.

groups.label: Failed assault on Quebec
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report (25 January 1776) of the unsuccessful attempt to take Quebec by storm on 31 December 1775.

groups.label: Letter from the camp before Quebec
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from the American camp before Quebec, dated 6 April 1776, on the batteries and the want of men. It circulated in two versions.

groups.label: Boston evacuated
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from headquarters at Cambridge, 19 March 1776, reporting that the British army left Boston on 17 March.

groups.label: Barry takes the Edward
groups.definition: Printings of Captain John Barry's letter to John Hancock or the Marine Committee ('In sight of the Capes of Virginia, April 7, 1776'): he fell in with the sloop Edward, belonging to the Liverpool frigate, and took her after a fight of near two glasses.

groups.label: The sloop Liberty's gunpowder taken
groups.definition: Printings of a Williamsburg report (13 April 1776) that on 30 March the sloop Liberty of Perth Amboy, from St. Eustatius with 83 barrels of gunpowder, dry goods and medicines, was taken by a British tender off the capes and carried into Norfolk, with what her mate, who escaped, said of British troops at Antigua.

groups.label: Hopkins's report from New Providence
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of Commodore Esek Hopkins's letter of 9 April 1776 to the President of Congress, on the fleet's expedition to New Providence in the Bahamas.

groups.label: Henry Stuart's letter to the frontier inhabitants, May 1776
groups.definition: Printings of a letter to the settlers on the Watauga and Nolachucky rivers, signed 'Henry Stuart, Deputy Superintendent', for the British superintendent of Indian affairs in the southern district, with a sworn statement that a stranger delivered it on 18 May 1776. The letter invites those 'willing to join his Majesty's forces, as soon as they arrive at the Cherokee nation' to sign a paper of allegiance, and says that the King will land an army in West Florida and march it through the Creek nation to the Chickasaws, 'where 500 warriors from each nation are to join them', and on by the Cherokees, 'who have also promised their assistance'. The papers printed it in June and July as a letter delivered to the frontier inhabitants, and from late August among papers sent from Augusta, Georgia, as 'an intercepted letter'. One side's letter, as printed.

groups.label: A letter from Savannah River, 13 May 1776: the Creek chiefs and the Cherokee towns
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Savannah River dated 13 May 1776, printed from Charleston (31 May): the writer reports that the Creek chiefs who were expected 'are down, and seem well disposed', and that letters from the Cherokees say the middle and lower towns will have no hand in it 'if the Over-hills are for mischief with the white people'; Henry Stewart and Captains Colbert and Gist (printed with the long s, 'Giſt', which the transcriptions read as 'Gift') are in the Over-hills with ammunition brought up the Mississippi, and were attacked on the way by 'the northward Indians'. One writer's report.

groups.label: Campbell's letter after his capture
groups.definition: Printings of Lieutenant Colonel Campbell's letter to General Howe (Boston, 19 June 1776), reporting that he and two companies of Highlanders had been taken in Boston harbour.

groups.label: British warships in the Hudson
groups.definition: Reports of the British warships that went up the Hudson on 12 July 1776: lying in Haverstraw Bay, boats driven off at Tappan, the attack by American row galleys (3 August) and the fire-ship attack (16 August). Contains those four groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: Warships in Haverstraw Bay
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report (24 July 1776) that the men of war lie in Haverstraw Bay, that a tender was fired on, and that a landing party was attacked at Peekskill.

groups.label: Boats driven off at Tappan
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report (end of July 1776) that about fifteen inhabitants drove off five boats from the men of war trying to land on Tappan meadows.

groups.label: Row galleys attack the warships
groups.definition: Printings of an eyewitness account of the attack by American row galleys (gondolas) on the Phoenix and the Rose on 3 August 1776.

groups.label: Fire-ship attack
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report of the fire-ship attack on the British ships in the Hudson on 16 August 1776.

groups.label: Washington meets Colonel Patterson
groups.definition: Printings of the account of the interview of 20 July 1776 between General Washington and Colonel Patterson, General Howe's adjutant general.

groups.label: Congress orders 88 battalions
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 16 September 1776 to raise eighty-eight battalions to serve during the war, with each state's quota and the bounties, plus one condensed report.

groups.label: Intelligence received in Congress, October 1776
groups.definition: Printings of the 'Intelligence received in Congress, October 21st, from the Middle and Northern Departments': General Mercer's raid on Staten Island and Arnold's fleet engaging the British on Lake Champlain on 11 October.

groups.label: Gates on Carleton's retreat
groups.definition: Printings of General Gates's letter to the President of Congress (Ticonderoga, 5 November 1776), published by order of Congress, reporting that General Carleton's fleet and army had withdrawn from Crown Point.

groups.label: The King's speech of October 1775
groups.definition: Printings of George III's speech opening the session of Parliament in October 1775, which the American papers printed from January 1776. The printings date the speech differently: the 26th in one, the 27th in another.

groups.label: Wilkes's speech in the Commons
groups.definition: Printings of the speech of John Wilkes, Lord Mayor of London, in the House of Commons on the motion for an address to the King at the opening of the session in October 1775, against the war in America.

groups.label: Governor Penn before the Lords
groups.definition: Reports of the examination of Richard Penn, former governor of Pennsylvania, who had carried Congress's petition to the King, in the House of Lords in November 1775, as the American papers printed them from February 1776: a short London report, and a long account with the questions and answers. Contains those two groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: A London report: Penn examined
groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of November 1775: on Friday Governor Penn was examined in the Upper Assembly and 'gave very satisfactory answers', and a member then proposed Congress's last petition to the King as the basis of an accommodation.

groups.label: The Lords examine Governor Penn
groups.definition: Printings of a London account of the House of Lords on 10 November 1775: the examination of Richard Penn, with the questions put to him and his answers, and the Duke of Richmond's motion grounded on them.

groups.label: The Prohibitory bill in the Commons
groups.definition: Reports from London of the bill to prohibit all trade and intercourse with the colonies (the Prohibitory Act) in the House of Commons in December 1775, as printed in February and March 1776: the debate in committee, which printed the clause on captures with blanks for its dates, and the clause as settled. Contains those two groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: The Commons in committee on the bill
groups.definition: Printings of a London report (6 December 1775) of the House of Commons in committee on the bill to prohibit all trade and intercourse with the colonies: the divisions, Lord North's remark on the clause that gives American ships time, and that clause printed with blanks for its dates, 'that the friends of America may have an opportunity' to have them filled with distant ones.

groups.label: The clause on captures settled
groups.definition: Printings of a London report (8 December 1775) that the clause of the bill which caused the greatest debate was settled: American ships to be captured from 1 January 1776, and all ships trading with the colonies from 1 June 1776.

groups.label: A Dublin paper: British force coming
groups.definition: Printings of news brought to Philadelphia in May 1776 by a passenger from Europe with a Dublin paper of 2 March: that a large naval force was coming to America and was ordered to sail on 10 April, followed by London paragraphs from that paper. The forecast is a report, not an observed event.

groups.label: Ethan Allen at Cork
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Cork (January 1776) on the gifts collected for Colonel Ethan Allen and his fellow prisoners in the Solebay, with Allen's note of thanks.

groups.label: London's address to the King
groups.definition: Printings of the City of London's address and petition to the King against the war (St. James's, 22 March 1776), with the King's answer.

groups.label: The King's speech of May 1776
groups.definition: Printings of George III's speech closing the session of Parliament on 23 May 1776.

groups.label: The Howe brothers' declarations
groups.definition: The declarations of Lord Howe and General William Howe as the King's commissioners for restoring peace, as the American papers printed them: Lord Howe's declaration of June 1776, published by order of Congress in July, and the brothers' declaration of 19 September. Contains those two groups; their declaration of 14 July (printed in the New-York Gazette) and their proclamation of 30 November (printed in the Freeman's Journal) are not included.

groups.label: Lord Howe's declaration, published by Congress
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 19 July 1776 ordering that Lord Howe's circular letter to the former royal governors (20 June 1776) and the declaration it enclosed be published, 'that the good people of these United States may be informed of what nature are the Commissioners, and what the terms', followed by the letter and the declaration offering pardons.

groups.label: The declaration of 19 September
groups.definition: Printings of the declaration of Lord Howe and General William Howe, the King's commissioners, of 19 September 1776: Congress had disavowed every purpose of reconciliation, the King would revise his instructions and the acts complained of, and the inhabitants were invited to consider whether to trust their fate to Congress.

groups.label: Congress on refusing Continental bills
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 11 January 1776 that anyone who refused the Continental bills of credit, or discouraged their circulation, should be treated as an enemy of his country.

groups.label: Congress's fast day of 17 May
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 16 March 1776 recommending that Friday 17 May be kept throughout the colonies as a day of humiliation, fasting and prayer. Includes a one-sentence notice of it and a New York committee's notice that quotes it.

groups.label: Congress opens the ports
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolutions of 6 April 1776 opening American ports to trade with all countries not under the British crown.

groups.label: Rhode Island renounces allegiance
groups.definition: Printings of the Rhode Island General Assembly's act of May 1776 repealing the act that secured allegiance to the King and putting the colony's name in place of his in commissions and writs.

groups.label: Congress's resolution of 15 May
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 15 May 1776, with its preamble, recommending that the colonies adopt governments under the authority of the people. Includes printings that quote it in full in reports of other bodies' proceedings.

groups.label: Virginia Convention, 15 May 1776
groups.definition: Printings of the Virginia Convention's resolutions of 15 May 1776, which instructed the colony's delegates to propose that Congress declare the colonies free and independent states.

groups.label: Pennsylvania's new instructions
groups.definition: Printings of the Pennsylvania Assembly's instructions of 8 June 1776 to its delegates in Congress, which withdrew the November instruction to reject any proposal that might lead to separation from Great Britain.

groups.label: Declaration of Independence
groups.definition: Printings of the Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776), plus one printing of its conclusion with a summary a week before that paper printed the full text.

groups.label: Congress on the Cedars cartel
groups.definition: Printings of the report adopted by Congress on 10 July 1776 on the cartel General Arnold agreed with Captain Foster after the surrender at the Cedars, with its resolutions.

groups.label: Prize resolutions extended
groups.definition: Printings of Congress's resolution of 24 July 1776 extending its earlier resolutions on captured ships and goods to all subjects of the King of Great Britain, except the inhabitants of the Bermudas and the Bahamas.

groups.label: Staten Island peace conference
groups.definition: Reports of the meeting of a committee of Congress (Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge) with Lord Howe on Staten Island in September 1776: their setting off, and the committee's report to Congress. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: Committee sets off to meet Lord Howe
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report (September 1776) that Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge had set off for New York to confer with Lord Howe.

groups.label: Committee's report on the conference
groups.definition: Printings of the committee's report to Congress on its meeting with Lord Howe on Staten Island, published by order of Congress in September 1776.

observations.excerpt: PHILADELPHIA, January 25. The last letters from Canada bring an account of an unsuccessful attempt made to gain possession of Quebec by storm, on the thirty-first of December last, between the hours of two and seven in the morning. The General finding his cannon too light to effect a breach, and that the enemy would not hearken to terms of capitulation, formed a design of carrying the town by escalade.

groups.label: Brussels, 17 October 1792: the emigrant princes' armies disbanded
groups.definition: Printings of a Brussels paragraph of 17 October 1792, printed in American papers in January and February 1793: word from the provinces of Namur and Luxembourg that the army of the French princes, Monsieur and the Count (or Duke) d'Artois, and that under the Duke de Bourbon were disbanded, and that their men wandered in great distress. A report ('We hear').

groups.label: Dumouriez's letter on entering Brussels, 14 November 1792
groups.definition: Printings of General Dumouriez's letter to the President of the National Convention, dated Brussels, 14 November 1792, and read in the Convention on 22 November: the Austrians had disputed the heights of Anderlecht with his advanced guard, and he had entered Brussels. One army's own account.

groups.label: The kings, princes and states at war with France
groups.definition: Printings of a list from a London paper of early April 1793 of the powers combined against France, from the King of Great Britain and the Empress of Russia to the princes of the Empire. Three papers print it as 'An account of the Kings, Princes, and States engaged against the Republic of France', three as 'a list of the combination of Kings, Princes, and States, at war with France', a combination 'without example in the annals of mankind'; the list is counted as one item. A report.

groups.label: Dumouriez's defection, April 1793
groups.definition: News of General Dumouriez's break with the National Convention in April 1793, as American papers printed it from late May: Clairfayt's letter that Dumouriez had sent the Convention's commissioners to the Austrian camp as prisoners, a London rumour that he had left his army, his own address to the French nation, and the Prince of Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation in support of it. Contains those four groups.

groups.label: Clairfayt's letter from Tournay: the commissioners sent as prisoners
groups.definition: Printings of a letter of the Austrian general Clairfayt to Count Starhemberg, the Imperial minister at The Hague (dated Tournay, 31 March 1793; some papers date it 3 April): Dumouriez had written to him that he had sent to the Austrian camp, as prisoners, General Bournonville and the commissioners whom the Convention had sent to arrest him. One side's account of what Dumouriez wrote.

groups.label: The Sun of 10 April: Dumouriez rumoured to have left his army
groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London Sun of 10 April 1793: it was rumoured that Dumouriez, having found reason to doubt his army's promises to support his plan of marching to Paris and placing young Louis on the throne, had left it at the head of a regiment of cavalry. A rumour, labelled as one. Several papers print it with a New York introduction ('In the Sun, of the 10th April, which is the latest paper received'), the others among London paragraphs.

groups.label: Dumouriez's address to the French nation, 2 April 1793
groups.definition: Printings of General Dumouriez's address 'to the French Nation', dated the Baths of St. Amand, 2 April 1793, printed from London papers: his services since the Revolution, his charges against the Convention and the Jacobins, his plan to restore the constitution with his army, and his oath to give up every public function afterwards. One side's account and a policy argument.

groups.label: The Prince of Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation to the French, 5 April 1793
groups.definition: Printings of the proclamation 'to the French' of the Austrian commander, the Prince of Saxe-Cobourg (Mons, 5 April 1793): he supported Dumouriez's declaration to the French nation, would act only as an auxiliary, and would hold any fortress handed to him only as a sacred trust. He withdrew these pledges in a proclamation of 9 April, which the same papers printed beside it.

groups.label: The London Gazette from Tournai, 3 May: the French attacks repulsed
groups.definition: Printings of a bulletin from the London Gazette, dated Tournai, 3 May 1793: on the 1st the French attacked the advanced posts of the left wing and of the centre of the combined army and were repulsed, with the loss of men and cannon. The British government's own account. Four papers print it after another Tournai paragraph on the preparations against Condé.

groups.label: The commissioners' letter on General Dampierre's death
groups.definition: Printings of a letter from the commissioners of the National Convention with the army of the North, Valenciennes, 9 May 1793, read in the Convention: General Dampierre, whose thigh was carried away by a ball the day before, died that morning, regretted by the whole army. The French government's commissioners' own account.

groups.label: The President of the National Convention's declaration of a plot
groups.definition: Printings of the 'Declaration made by the President of the National Convention to the French Nation' (Paris, May 1793): after a scandalous scene in the galleries, he declared his conviction of a conspiracy, revealed to him by good citizens, to destroy the Convention, and his resolve to wait the event at his post. One man's declaration of an alleged plot.

groups.label: News from Cap Français, June 1793
groups.definition: Two accounts of events at Cap Français, in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, from 18 to 23 June 1793, as American papers printed them in July and August from arrivals at New York: Captain Fanning's account, and the report of the passengers of the brig Mary, who put the dead at six to nine hundred, 'instead of 10 thousand as we heard', as most papers print it. Contains those two groups; the wider coverage is not included. Each is an account at second hand.

groups.label: Captain Fanning's account of Cap Français
groups.definition: Printings of the account given at New York by Captain John Fanning of the brig Union, 14 days from Cap Français (New York, 9 July 1793): on 18 June the civil commissioners Sonthonax and Polverel arrived at the Cape and suspended the governor, Galbaud; by his account they then encouraged 'a number of mulattoes' to come into town, who armed the enslaved people of the town 'to assist in destroying all the whites'; between 8 and 10 thousand people were killed from 20 June; and the town was plundered and burnt, with not more than 50 houses standing when he sailed on the 23rd with a fleet of 250 sail. One ship captain's account. Three papers print it under the heading 'HORRID NEWS!'.

groups.label: The brig Mary's passengers on Cap Français
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report of late July 1793 on the brig Mary, Captain Langdon, from Cap Français, which she left on 9 July: her forty passengers said that from six to nine hundred people lost their lives 'in the affair of the 20th' (most papers add 'instead of 10 thousand as we heard'; the Patowmac Guardian prints 'two thousand'), that not more than two thirds of the town was burnt, that 'upwards of 20,000 mulattoes and blacks are now under arms there', that 'the negroes never came in from the country on the late occasion', and that the Spaniards had taken a town and were on the march. The passengers' account, at second hand.

groups.label: A letter from Cadiz, 24 June: 'a hot war with the Spaniards and French'
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Cadiz to his brother in New York, dated 24 June 1793 (New York, 12 August): 'a hot war with the Spaniards and French', a battle near Malaga reported won by the French, and news of the fleets. One writer's account, partly hearsay ('We had accounts').

groups.label: By the brig Molly from Madeira: a battle near Lisle reported
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 14 August 1793: by the brig Molly, Capt. Morris, from Madeira, word that a frigate from Falmouth had brought English papers to about 24 June with an account of a very bloody battle near Lisle, to the advantage of the French, in which 17,000 men fell; Morris said the account was believed at Madeira. A report at third hand of what newspapers said; the Gazette of the United States and the American Herald of Liberty add that the consul's letter from Madeira of 4 July said there was nothing new.

groups.label: A letter from German Creek, 16 August 1793: an expedition across the Tennessee
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter dated German Creek, Territory South of the Ohio, 16 August 1793, written to the editor of a Winchester paper (2 September) and printed from it: the writer reports that on 4 August Colonel Daugherty of Jefferson county crossed the Tennessee with 180 men to 'the valley Indian towns', where by his account they killed nine men and two women, took seven prisoners, burnt twenty towns and villages and destroyed crops, with five of their own men wounded. He adds that the frontier inhabitants are 'in close forts', and argues for a large company raised 'under the sanction of government' to give the towns, in his words, 'a severe flogging, in order to bring them to a sense of their duty, and teach them to pay some respect to treaties'. One writer's account.

groups.label: The War Office on the treaty commissioners, September 1793
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of early September 1793: by an express to the War Office from the commissioners for treating with the Indian nations north of the Ohio, they 'were not able even to effect a meeting' with the nations assembled at the rapids of the Miami river; the nations' deputation 'insisted upon the Ohio as the boundary between them and the United States', and, 'as so extensive a concession was inadmissible', the commissioners left on 17 August. It names the Wyandots, Delawares, Shawanese and Miamis as 'determined for war', says that a considerable part of them were for peace, and that the Six Nations, with Captain Brandt (Brant) and his Mohawks, urged peace. The United States government's account, as the papers printed it.

groups.label: Captain Crabtree's sea serpent
groups.definition: Printings of a Portland (District of Maine) paragraph of 3 August 1793 headed 'Sea Monster': Captain Crabtree, lately arrived at Frenchman's Bay, says that on 20 June, on his passage from the West Indies and in sight of Mount Desert island, he watched for nearly an hour a serpent of enormous size, which he judged to be 55 to 60 feet long, its head raised six or eight feet out of the water. One man's account, which the paper says 'may be depended on'.

groups.label: Hamilton's circular to the collectors, with the President's rules on neutrality
groups.definition: Printings of the circular of the Secretary of the Treasury to the collectors of the customs (Philadelphia, 4 August 1793): as repeated contraventions of neutrality had taken place in American ports, the collectors were to watch for vessels arming or equipping for the powers at war, with the schedule of 'Rules adopted by the President' on arming, equipping and prizes. The circular and its rules are one publication. An official document.

groups.label: Genêt and the President: the 'appeal to the people', 1793
groups.definition: One affair in three printed documents, as the papers printed them from mid-August to early September 1793: John Jay and Rufus King's statement that the French minister, Genêt, had said he would appeal to the people from certain decisions of the President; Genêt's letter to the President asking him to declare that he had never said so to him; and the Secretary of State's answer for the President. Contains those three groups. The statement is an allegation and the letter the minister's own account; whether he said it is not settled here.

groups.label: Jay and King: Genêt said he would appeal to the people
groups.definition: Printings of a card of John Jay and Rufus King to the printers of the New York Diary (August 1793): a report having reached New York from Philadelphia that Mr. Genêt, the French minister, had said he would appeal to the people from certain decisions of the President, they had been asked on their return whether he had said so, and 'we answered, that he had'. An allegation by two named men.

groups.label: Genêt's letter to the President, 13 August 1793
groups.definition: Printings of the letter of Citizen Genêt, minister plenipotentiary of the French Republic, to President Washington (New York, 13 August 1793), printed with the Secretary of State's answer, as published in New York (the National Gazette credits the New York Diary of 21 August): persons were saying that he had threatened to appeal to the people from the President's decisions, and he asked the President for an explicit declaration that he had never intimated such an intention to him. The minister's own account.

groups.label: Jefferson's answer for the President, 16 August 1793
groups.definition: Printings of the Secretary of State's answer to Genêt for the President (Philadelphia, 16 August 1793): the diplomatic characters residing here should not correspond directly with the President, the Secretary of State being the organ of their communications, and the President did not think it within the line of propriety or duty to bear evidence against a declaration, so he declined to interfere. An official document.

groups.label: Boyd / Bantry coverage
groups.definition: Reports, printed challenge and later related account concerning the expedition; not a single verified event.

groups.label: Boyd fleet report
groups.definition: Corresponding core fleet report; includes the edition with an appended challenge.

groups.label: Later fleet-return account
groups.definition: Later related account concerning the main body returning to Brest; no explicit retraction assigned.

groups.label: Tenerife defeat report
groups.definition: Printings of a Norfolk report, from a passenger on the Danish ship Christian Haven, that the British attack on Santa Cruz de Tenerife (July 1797) was driven off. Other Tenerife accounts in the collection are different texts and are not included.

groups.label: Duncan's Camperdown dispatches
groups.definition: Printings of Admiral Duncan's official dispatches on the defeat of the Dutch fleet off Camperdown (11 October 1797), from the London Gazette Extraordinary. Earlier first-news reports are not included.

groups.label: Algerine–Sicilian sea battle
groups.definition: Printings of a Civitavecchia report (30 June 1797) of a battle near Messina between an Algerine cruiser and a ship of the King of the Two Sicilies. The battle itself is not independently verified.

groups.label: Hermione mutiny
groups.definition: Reports of the mutiny on the British frigate Hermione (September 1797) and her delivery to the Spanish at La Guaira: first rumours, the detailed 'Particulars', and a follow-up.

groups.label: 'Particulars of the mutiny'
groups.definition: Printings of the detailed account of the Hermione mutiny first printed in Philadelphia on 16 November 1797.

groups.label: Barney escapes the blockade
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of Commodore Barney's letter of 21 August 1797 on escaping a seven-month blockade.

groups.label: Sonthonax leaves Saint-Domingue
groups.definition: Reports (September–October 1797) that the commissioner Sonthonax had sailed for France and Toussaint Louverture held the chief command.

groups.label: Quito earthquake
groups.definition: Printings of a Quito account (6 February 1797), via Jamaica, of the earthquake of 4 February.

groups.label: Peace / Cayenne context
groups.definition: Research collection of a seizure report and decree/commentary. Membership does not assert a legal or causal link.

groups.label: Peace seizure report
groups.definition: Corresponding reports about the named Peace account attributed to Whitney; excludes unresolved later same-name leads.

groups.label: Cayenne decree and commentary
groups.definition: Printed translated decree and attached allegation; original decree and itemized allegations remain unresolved.

groups.label: Peace and Plenty boarding
groups.definition: Printed accounts of the brig Peace and Plenty (Capt. Dunbar) being boarded and plundered by a French privateer, October 1797. A different vessel from the brig Peace (Capt. Allen). The accounts are not independently verified.

groups.label: Peace and Plenty report
groups.definition: Corresponding versions of the 'Piracy and Cruelty' marine report with Dunbar's quoted statement. Excludes the condensed 16 October retelling.

groups.label: Brothers boarded by privateer
groups.definition: Printings of Captain Kennard's report that the brig Brothers was boarded by a privateer on the way from Grenada to Portsmouth, N.H. (September 1797). Not independently verified.

groups.label: Two Sisters wreck
groups.definition: Printed accounts of the Rhode Island ship Two Sisters found wrecked off Bantry Bay in August 1797: a reprinted hand-bill and a summary attributed to the Irish papers. Different wording; the wreck itself is not independently verified.

groups.label: French captures at Havana
groups.definition: Printings of a Charleston report (September 1797) that more than a hundred American vessels had been carried into Havana by French privateers.

groups.label: Adams's farewell to the Senate
groups.definition: Printings of Vice President Adams's farewell address to the Senate (15 February 1797), plus the Senate's answer where printed separately.

groups.label: Special session of Congress, 1797
groups.definition: The special session of 1797: Adams's summoning proclamation (25 March), his speech (16 May) and the House's answer. Contains the speech, proclamation and answer groups.

groups.label: Adams's speech to Congress
groups.definition: Printings of President Adams's speech of 16 May 1797 opening the special session of Congress. Pages that only quote phrases from it are not included.

groups.label: Proclamation summoning Congress
groups.definition: Printings of Adams's proclamation of 25 March 1797 convening Congress on 15 May.

groups.label: House's answer to the special-session speech
groups.definition: Printings of the House of Representatives' answer to Adams's speech of 16 May 1797, in draft and final form.

groups.label: Blount affair
groups.definition: The Blount affair in the 1797 papers: the letter made public (July), Blount's welcome home at Knoxville (September), and the House committee's report (December). Contains those three groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: Blount letter made public
groups.definition: Printings of Senator William Blount's intercepted letter to the interpreter James Carey (July 1797): the letter as a document, and a Philadelphia report that introduces and quotes it. The wider Blount affair coverage is not included.

groups.label: Blount's welcome at Knoxville
groups.definition: Printings of a Knoxville report (18 September 1797) of Blount's welcome home.

groups.label: House committee report on Blount
groups.definition: Reports of the House committee's evidence report on Blount, 4 December 1797: a fuller account and a shorter summary.

groups.label: Andrew Brown house fire
groups.definition: Reports of the fire at the Philadelphia house of the printer Andrew Brown (27 January 1797) and notices of his death a week later. Several different texts.

groups.label: Opening of Congress, November 1797
groups.definition: Printings of Adams's speech opening the second session of the Fifth Congress (23 November 1797), the Senate's and House's answers, and his reply to the House.

groups.label: Kościuszko's land warrant
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia item (September 1797): Kościuszko is offered a land warrant and back pay for his Revolutionary War service and declines the money.

groups.label: Jefferson's letter to Madison
groups.definition: Reports (January 1797) that Jefferson wrote to Madison about the election result, and a later report giving a different account of the letter.

groups.label: New Hampshire governor's address
groups.definition: Printings of the New Hampshire governor's address to the legislature, 22 November 1797.

observations.excerpt: Captain Boye positively asserts, that previous to his failing, accounts were received at the custom-house of Liverpool, of 17 sail of French vessels, men of war and transports, having a number of troops on board, destined for a descent on Ireland, being through gusts of weather blown into Bantry Bay, most of them distressed; some of the people went on shore, were made prisoners, and sent to Dublin; from the situation of the place the whole must inevitably be captured. They intended to have effected a landing at Londonderry in the North of Ireland.
observations.summary: Boyd's account of the French fleet at Bantry Bay.
observations.note: Scan: dismasted; RevX: distressed. The capture statement is a prediction.

observations.excerpt: Capt. Boyd, positively asserts, that previous to his sailing, accounts were received at the custom house of Liverpool, of 17 sail of French vessels, men of war and transports, having a number of troops on board, destined for a DESCENT ON IRELAND, being through stress of weather, blown into Bantry Bay, most of them dismasted; some of the people went on shore, were made prisoners, and went to Dublin; from the situation of the place the whole must inevitably be captured. They intended to have effected a landing at Londonderry in the North of Ireland. [NOTE. Capt. Boyd failed from Liverpool on the 29th December, and the French fleet left Brest, on the 26th of the same month: How then is it possible they should have reached Ireland in 3 days, and the accounts from thence received at Liverpool? Can it be thought that 20,000 French troops, and 17 ships of the line, have surrendered to the inhabitants of Bantry, whose population does not exceed 10,000 souls? It is more natural to think the French have taken that town.—Why were those 20,000 French sent to Dublin, 154 miles from Bantry Bay, and not to Cork, that lies but 9 miles from it? Can it be presumed, that the French fleet, in order to effect a landing at Londonderry, had entered the channel of Ireland so full of dangers, instead of sailing westward, on the main; a route much shorter and less difficult, free from the dangers of the channel, and which would not have exposed them to discovery from Liverpool or Dublin, and meet with every obstacle, that could have frustrated their design. CHRONICLE.]
observations.summary: The report appears with an appended challenge.
observations.note: Printed CHRONICLE challenge; objections are not independently adjudicated. Some failed forms read sailed in the scan.

observations.excerpt: Of the intelligence brought by the late arrivals, the most important relates to the French expedition against Ireland. By comparing the various accounts it appears, that the French failed from Brest with a view of invading Ireland. Their force consisted of about 50 sail, including transports, of which 17 were of the line and about 25,000 men on board. They failed in three divisions, under the command of De Galle, Bouvet and Neilly; the land troops under the orders of Gen. Hoche. They had scarcely left the port when bad weather dispersed them. Chief part of the fleet however, rendezvoused at Bantry Bay, but the frigate la Fraternite, on board of which were the commanders of the fleet and land forces not joining the fleet, after some delay they left the bay without molestation, except from the winds and by the best and latest accounts, reached Brest in divisions, without material loss. The Fraternite was one of the vessels to return. The expedition appears to have caused great alarm in Ireland and England. Had not the elements conspired against the French, little doubt can be entertained but they would have been successful. The expedition appears to have been planned on a large scale. The Toulon fleet which came round to L'Orient, and the armament at Dunkirk were probably to co-operate. The French appear still to have an expedition to Ireland in contemplation. A Paris date of January 29, mentions the arrival of Gen. Hoche in that capital, to give an account of his expedition.
observations.summary: Two weeks after printing Boyd's capture prediction, the Patowmac Guardian prints a summary saying the fleet dispersed and returned to Brest.
observations.note: The same summary the Kentucky Gazette printed on 19 April (H007), here 20 days earlier under a Martinsburg dateline. Neither paper names a source, so the copying route is unknown. The wording differs: Kentucky adds 'We have collected under this head…' and 'Notwithstanding the above failure'; this version adds the Fraternité's return, the 'great alarm' sentences and a Paris date about Hoche.

observations.excerpt: Of the intelligence brought by the late arrivals, the most important relates to the French expedition against Ireland. We have collected under this head, every interesting detail we have been able to meet with. By comparing the various accounts, it appears, that the French force when it failed from Brest, consisted of about 50 sail, including transports, of which 17 were of the line, and had on board 25,000 men.—They failed in three divisions, under the command of De Galles, Bouvet and Neuilly; the land troops under the command of general Hoche. They had scarcely left the port when bad weather dispersed them. Chief part of the fleet however rendezvoused at Bantry Bay, but the frigate la Fraternite, on board of which were the commanders of the fleet and land forces, not joining the fleet, after some delay left the Bay, without molestation, except by the wind, and by the best and latest accounts, reached Brest, in divisions without material loss. The expedition appears to have been planned on a large scale. The Toulon fleet which came round to l'Orient, and the armament at Dunkirk were probably to co-operate. Notwithstanding the above failure, the French appear still to have an expedition to Ireland in contemplation.

observations.excerpt: It is easy to perceive, that the American papers, cited in this decree, are the Jacobin Gazettes of the United States, and that the instances quoted, are seven out of eight, false and scandalous. It is also very evident, that the French Agents, in the United States, have published those very accounts in the Aurora , Argus , Chronicle , and other hiring papers, merely to give a pretext to the plunderers in the West-Indies, to seize and confiscate American vessels, and that the Printers of them have been base and sordid enough to send them those papers, in order that they may be adduced as documents, to justify their infamy! The American merchants and seamen, who suffer under the piracies in the West-Indies, now look to those Printers as the Authors of their misery; and were they to prosecute for reparation, an honest jury would do no less than grant a verdict in their favor.
observations.summary: A translated Cayenne decree with an attached editorial allegation.
observations.note: A contextual document, not an established legal cause of the Peace seizure. The original decree and itemized allegations remain unresolved.

observations.excerpt: PIRACY AND CRUELTY. Same day, brig Peace and Plenty, Dunbar, St. Croix, 24 days. In lat. 23, N. long. 65, 35, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, under English colours. The particulars of the treatment which capt. D. received, is thus recorded by him.
observations.summary: Captain Dunbar of the brig Peace and Plenty reports being boarded and plundered by a French privateer from Guadeloupe.
observations.note: The scan prints Dunbar's full quoted statement (about 350 words) after this introduction. The RevX transcription drops it; the CA transcription keeps it. The excerpt is limited to the RevX text, so read the statement on the scan.

observations.excerpt: BOSTON, OCT. 11. Fraternity.—Capt. Dunbar, from St. Croix, in lat. 23, N. long. 65, 35, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, the capt. of which, with five of his crew, came on board and demanded Capt. D's papers; after examination, ordered his chests and trunks to be opened— took from them all the money and letters— took all the flock cabin stores, spare rigging, sails and blocks—one cask of rum, &c. —suffered his people to steal even knives and forks, spoons, tumblers, and every article remaining in the cabin. The privateer captain put on board us two seamen taken from the brig Favourite, Scituate, of Baltimore, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. He also wished to get rid of Capt. Scituate and Mr. Taylor, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer and know the state of their property, which spirited behaviour produced a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer, the capt. indignantly flogged them! Several other American masters and seamen were on board this privateer, among them was Mr. John Barnes, of Marblehead. Before the privateer left us, she took a loop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape-Francois. The captain of the privateer to finish his brutal behaviour, threatened to punish capt. Dunbar—dismissed him with a curse on his country, and a determination to rob every American vessel that could not be made a prize of.
observations.summary: Three days later the same paper prints a shorter retelling of Dunbar's account under a Boston, Oct. 11 dateline, headed 'Fraternity'.
observations.note: A condensed paraphrase rather than the quoted statement, so it belongs to the boarding group but not the core report group.

observations.excerpt: Same day, brig Peace and Plenty, Dunbar, St. Croix, 24 days. In lat. 23, N. long. 65, 55, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, under English colors. The particulars of the treatment which Capt. D. received, is thus recorded by him. "The capt. of this privateer came on board, with five of his crew, and demanded my papers; after examination, ordered all my trunks and chests to be opened, and took from them all the money they contained, with the letters, which he opened; he took all our stock, and cabin stores, with all the spare running rigging, sails and blocks, and cut one studling-fall from the yard; he also took one cask of rum, belonging to the cargo, and a case that belonged to capt. Haynes, who was to have come passenger, contents unknown. After plundering us of the above articles, he suffered his people to rob us of what they pleased, and so fully devoted were they to the business of thieving, that they took every article they could find, even to the knives, forks, spoons and tumblers, and in fact every article remaining in the cabin.—He then put two seamen on board, that were taken a few days before from the brig Favorite, Sisson, of Baltimore, master, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. The capt. of the privateer, wished to put capt. Sisson, and Mr. Taylor on board my vessel, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer, and demanded to know the fate of their property, which spirited behaviour produced on the commander of the privateer, a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer he inhumanly flogged them! Besides capt. Sisson, there were several other American masters and seamen on board the privateer, names, except one, not to be ascertained, this individual's name was John Barnes, of Marblehead:—A few hours previous to our being boarded, the privateer took a sloop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape Francois, who, he said, was a good prize. To add insult to our misfortune this inhuman pirate threatened to take me on board his vessel, and inflict an ignominious punishment on me; and finished his brutal behaviour by dismissing me, with a curse on my country, and a declared determination to rob every American vessel he could not make a prize of.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the full report with Dunbar's quoted statement.
observations.note: Corresponds closely to the Gazette of the United States text of 13 October as printed on the scan.

observations.excerpt: Piracy and Cruelty. Arrived, brig Peace and Plenty, Dunbar, St. Caoix, 24 day. In lat. 23 N. long. 65. 35. W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadaloupe under English colours. The particulars of the treatment which Capt. D. received, are thus recorded by him. "The capt. of this privateer came on board, with five of his crew, and demanded my papers; after examination, ordered all my trunks and chests to be opened, and took from them all the money they contained, with the letters, which he opened; he took all our stock, and cabin stores, with all the spare running rigging, sails and blocks, and cut one fludding sail from the yard; he also took one cask of rum, belonging to the cargo, and a cask that belonged to Capt. Hayoc, who was to have come passenger, contents unknown. After plundering us of the above articles, he suffered his people to rob us of what they pleased; and fully devoted were they to the business of thieving, that they took every article they could find, even to the knives, forks, spoons, and tumblers, and in fact every article remaining in the cabin. He then put two seamen on board, who were taken a few days before from the brig Favorite, Siffon of Baltimore, master, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 30,000 dollars. The Capt. of the privateer wished to put Capt. Siffon, and Mr. Taylor on board my vessel; but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer, and demanded to know the fate of their property, which spirited behaviour produced on the commander of the privateer, a conduct unbecoming a man; for on their refusal to quit the privateer, he inhumanly fluted them! Besides Capt. Siffon, there were several other American masters and seamen on board the privateer, names, except one, not to be ascertained, this individual's name was John Barns, of Marsthead. A few hours previous to our being boarded, the privateer took a sloop from Rhode-Island, Captain Briggs, bound to Cape Francois, who, he said, was a good prize. To add insult to our misfortune, this inhuman pirate threatened to take me on board his vessel, and inflict an ignominious punishment on me; and finished his brutal behavior by dismissing me, with a curse on my country, and a declared determination to rob every American vessel he could not make a prize of."
observations.summary: The Eagle prints the full report under a Boston, Oct. 8 dateline.
observations.note: 'St. Caoix' and '24 day' are printed that way in the paper. The Eagle prints a Boston execution report directly after it; that story also appears in the New Hampshire Gazette of 17 October.

observations.excerpt: Dreadful SHIPWRECK!! The following account of the shipwreck of the Two Sisters of Rhode-Island, is taken from a Hand-Bill published at BANTRY-BAY, AUG. 12, '97. This morning about 2 o'clock, as some of our fishing boats were working out between the heads, they saw a large ship in the Offing, seemingly in great distress. They stood for the ship, and about 10 o'clock, they boarded her; but there was only one living man on board. She proves to be the Two Sisters, from Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, and had been out five weeks:—Such a wreck, surely never was seen before! her mizen-mast was all split to pieces, and her main-mast was a stern hanging by some of the wreck; her foremast was also split to pieces, and her fore-top-mast gone by the cap in her steerage or half deck. There were seven men burnt to a coal, and the mate lying under the windlass dead; and as for the Captain, we have no account of him, only the young man found with the wreck says that the Captain and all hands were on deck when some dreadful thunder and lightning came on; and that there were six men on the main-top-sail yard when the mainmast went over the side, and that they were all lost. He says the Captain was on the quarter deck when the mast went, but as he did not see him afterwards, he thinks the wreck hauled him overboard.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette reprints a Bantry Bay hand-bill dated 12 August 1797 on the wreck of the Rhode Island ship Two Sisters.
observations.note: Hand-bill account: lightning struck the ship, one man survived, seven men were burnt and the mate died. The captain is missing.

observations.excerpt: A melancholy narrative appears in the lists of the disasters of the American ship Two Sisters, of Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, off Bantry Bay, in August last. On appearance of distress, she was boarded by some people from the land—they found her mizen mast shivered to pieces, her main mast overboard, hanging astern, and her fore topsail gone by the cap—only one living man was found in the wreck, who informed that the ship had been struck by lightning, and that there were six men on the main topsail yard when the mainmast went over the side, all of whom were lost, together with the master of the vessel, who was wanted overboard—seven men were burnt to a coal, and the mate dead; the ship had four feet water in her hold when boarded—was from the Bay of Honduras, with oil, whale bone, logwood and mahogany; the captain's name Gilbert; owner Mr. Mosely of Rhode Island—the people of the coast hauled the vessel up on the beach; the bottom appeared to be in tolerable condition; but masts, spars, sails, &c. worth nothing.
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States summarizes the same wreck, citing the Irish papers, and adds the cargo, captain and owner.
observations.note: Different wording from the hand-bill, but the details correspond: six men on the main topsail yard, seven men burnt and the mate dead.

observations.excerpt: January 27. MELANCHOLLY AND DISTRESSING. This morning about a quarter before 6 o'clock, Fire broke out in the lower part of the Dwelling-House of Mr. Andrew Brown, Printer, of this city. The usual spirited exertions of the Citizens prevented the flames from extending to the adjoining houses—and Mr. Brown's Printing Office escaped uninjured. Every humane bosom must be wrung with anguish at the recital of the shocking catastrophe consequent to this event. Mr. Brown, his apprentices, and some other domestics of the family escaped with their lives, by rushing thro' the flames or jumping from the windows—Mr. Brown is very much bruised and is dangerously ill
observations.summary: First report of the fire at the Philadelphia house of the printer Andrew Brown on 27 January 1797.
observations.note: Found by phrase search, not by the reuse family. The report goes on to describe what happened to Mrs Brown and her three children.

observations.excerpt: The mournful tale of the dreadful catastrophe which lately overwhelmed the family of Mr. Brown, the printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, was heightened by the death of Mr. Brown himself, who expired on Saturday morning.
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States reports Andrew Brown's own death after the fire.
observations.note: A shorter, differently worded notice than the version the other papers carry.

observations.excerpt: PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 28. Melancholy Event. Never since we have assumed the office of recording passing events to the public, have we entered on the task with more painful sensations, than on the melancholy occasion we have now to mention. About 5 o'clock yesterday morning the house of Mr. ANDREW BROWN, Printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, was discovered to be on fire. How it originated or progressed, we have not correct information, but the melancholy and almost unparalleled catastrophe, is, we fear, too certain. Mrs. BROWN, two daughters, one son, and a negro boy, have perished in the flames. Two apprentices have suffered severely, and Mr. BROWN is so dreadfully burnt, that but faint hopes of his recovery are entertained.
observations.summary: A different Philadelphia report of the fire: it says Mrs Brown, two daughters, a son and a Black boy died in the flames.
observations.note: Found by phrase search. Different wording from the Patowmac Guardian report.

observations.excerpt: The mournful catastrophe which has lately overwhelmed the family of Mr. Brown, the printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, attained its full height on Saturday morning, by the death of Mr. Brown himself of an inflammation of the lungs, occasioned by the large quantity of smoke and mephitic air which he had inhaled, before he was extricated from the fire.
observations.summary: The Virginia Argus prints the longer notice of Brown's death.
