observations.excerpt: The Senate, in a body, this day waited on the President of the United States, with the following answer to his address to both Houses, at the opening of the present session. To the PRESIDENT of the United States. SIR, THE communications you have thought proper to make in your speech to both houses of Congress, on the opening of their session, afford additional proofs of the attention, integrity and firmness which have always marked your official character.
observations.summary: The Senate's answer to the speech.
observations.note: Printed the day it was presented.

observations.excerpt: Mr. OTIS, from the committee appointed to draft an address in answer to the speech of the President of the United States, reported the following, which was twice read, and referred to a committee of the whole for to-morrow: SIR, WHILE our sympathy is excited by the recent sufferings of the citizens of Philadelphia, we participate in the satisfaction which you are pleased to express, that the duration of the late calamity was so limited
observations.summary: The House committee's draft answer, opening with sympathy for Philadelphia's sufferings.
observations.note: The draft as first reported; the House amended it before passing.

observations.excerpt: To which the President made the following reply: Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I RECEIVE this address from the House of Representatives of the United States with peculiar pleasure.
observations.summary: Adams's reply to the House's answer.
observations.note: Printed the day after it was given.

observations.excerpt: On Thursday at 12 o'clock, the Senate having assembled in the Representatives' Hall, The President came in, accompanied by his Secretary and the Heads of Departments, and delivered the following SPEECH. Gentlemen of the Senate, and Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I WAS for some time apprehensive, that it would be necessary, on account of the contagious sickness which afflicted the city of Philadelphia, to convene the national Legislature, at some other place.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the speech.
observations.note: Same speech; only the opening is excerpted.

observations.excerpt: At 12 o'clock, the Senate having assembled in the Representatives' Hall, the President came in, accompanied by his Secretary and the heads of departments, and delivered the following SPEECH: Gentlemen of the Senate, and Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I WAS for some time apprehensive, that it would be necessary, on account of the contagious sickness which afflicted the city of Philadelphia, to convene the National Legislature, at some other place.
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the speech.
observations.note: The speech continues on page 3.

observations.excerpt: The following is the address of the Senate, in answer to the Speech delivered by the President of the United States, at the opening of the Session: TO THE PRESIDENT of the United States. SIR, THE communications you have thought proper to make in your Speech to both Houses of Congress on the opening of their present session, afford additional proofs of the attention, integrity, and firmness, which have always marked your official character.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the Senate's answer.
observations.note: Same page as the House's answer.

observations.excerpt: The Answer of the House stands as follows:— SIR, WHILE our sympathy is excited by the recent sufferings of the citizens of Philadelphia, we participate in the satisfaction which you are pleased to express, that the duration of the late calamity was so limited
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the House's answer as passed.
observations.note: After a report of the amendment debate.

observations.excerpt: The following is the Address of the Senate in answer to the Speech delivered by the President of the United States, at the opening of the session:— To the PRESIDENT of the U. STATES. SIR, THE communications you have thought proper to make in your speech, to both Houses of Congress, on the opening of their present session, afford additional proofs of the attention, integrity and firmness, which have always marked your official character.
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the Senate's answer.
observations.note: Same page as the House's answer.

observations.excerpt: Then answer was then reported to the House, and passed in the following words:— SIR, WHILE our sympathy is excited by the recent sufferings of the citizens of Philadelphia, we participate in the satisfaction which you are pleased to express; that the duration of the late calamity was so limited
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the House's answer as passed.
observations.note: After a report of the amendment debate.

observations.excerpt: The President's Reply, to the Answer of the House. Gentlemen of the House of Representatives, I RECEIVE this Address from the House of Representatives of the United States with peculiar pleasure.
observations.summary: The Mirror prints Adams's reply to the House.
observations.note: Follows Adams's reply to the Senate on the same page.

observations.excerpt: To which the President returned the following answer, Gentlemen of the House of Representatives. I received this address from the House of Representatives of the United States with peculiar pleasure.
observations.summary: The Eagle prints Adams's reply to the House.
observations.note: Same reply.

observations.excerpt: General Kosciusko, we hear, has left the city, on a visit to General White, of New Brunswick. Before he left town, we understand, a gentleman in office presented him with a land warrant, to which he was entitled by his services, and intimated there was a sum of money due to him, for his services in the cause of this country.
observations.summary: General Kościuszko, visiting Philadelphia, is offered a land warrant and back pay for his Revolutionary War service.
observations.note: Printed beside a yellow-fever burial report signed by Stephen Girard.

observations.excerpt: PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 6. General Kosciuszko, we hear, has left the city, on a visit to Gen. White, of New Brunswick. Before he left town, we understand, a gentleman in office presented him with a land warrant, to which he was entitled by his services, and intimated there was a sum of money due to him, for his services in the cause of this country.
observations.summary: The New Hampshire Gazette prints the same item.
observations.note: Same item.

observations.excerpt: General Kosciuszko, we hear, has left the city on a visit to his friend General Gates, in the state of New York. Before he left town, we understand, a gentleman in office presented him with a land warrant, to which he was entitled by his services, and intimated there was a sum of money due to him, for his services in the cause of this country.
observations.summary: The Kentucky Gazette prints the item.
observations.note: Says he left to visit 'his friend General Gates, in the state of New York', not General White of New Brunswick.

observations.excerpt: We are informed, and from an authority which we rely on, that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison on the subject of the late election; and given it as his opinion, that Mr. Adams was the only person who ought to have been elected President; and further, that he is the only person under whom he would accept the Vice-Presidency. If our information is accurate, the acceptance of Mr. J. will be unquestionable.
observations.summary: Report that Jefferson wrote to Madison that Adams alone ought to have been elected, and that he would serve as Vice President under him.
observations.note: No dateline in this printing.

observations.excerpt: BOSTON, January 14. We are informed, and from an authority which we rely on, that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison on the subject of the late election; and given it as his opinion, that Mr. Adams was the only person who ought to have been elected President; and further, that he is the only person under whom he would accept the Vice-Presidency. If our information is accurate, the acceptance of Mr. J. will be unquestionable.
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States prints the report under a Boston dateline.
observations.note: Same report.

observations.excerpt: STOCKBRIDGE, January 23. It is true that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison, requesting him, (for reasons which he details,) if there should be an equal vote between Mr. Adams and himself,
observations.summary: A Stockbridge report confirms the letter and gives a different account of what it asked.
observations.note: Different text: says the letter asked Madison to act if the vote was tied.

observations.excerpt: WASHINGTON CITY, January 28. We are informed, and from an authority which we rely on, that Mr. Jefferson has written to Mr. Madison on the subject of the late election; and given it as his opinion, that Mr. Adams was the only person who ought to have been elected President; and further, that he is the only person under whom he would accept the Vice-Presidency. If our information is accurate, the acceptance of Mr. Jefferson will be unquestion
observations.summary: The Patowmac Guardian prints the report under a Washington City dateline.
observations.note: Same report; spells out 'Mr. Jefferson' where others have 'Mr. J.'.

observations.excerpt: The honorable Senate being assembled with the House in the Representatives chamber, His Excellency the Governor came in, escorted by the committee, and delivered to both branches of the Legislature the following ADDRESS: Fellow citizens of the Senate, and of the House of Representatives. IN meeting you at this time when the tranquility, general health and prosperity of the State afford so much cause for mutual congratulation,
observations.summary: The New Hampshire governor's address opening the legislature's session, 22 November 1797.
observations.note: Printed in the legislature's journal.

observations.excerpt: The Senate being assembled with the House in the Representatives' Chamber, His Excellency the Governor came in, escorted by the committee, and delivered to both branches of the Legislature the following ADDRESS. Fellow Citizens of the Senate, and of the House of Representatives, IN meeting you at this time, when tranquility, general health and prosperity of the State afford so much cause for mutual congratulation,
observations.summary: The Mirror prints the governor's address.
observations.note: Same address.

observations.excerpt: PORTSMOUTH, (N.H.) Nov. 25. On Wednesday last agreeably to adjournment, the Hon. General Court convened in this town. The Hon. Senate being assembled with the house in the representatives chamber, His Excellency the Governor came in escorted by the committee, and addressed the Legislature with the following SPEECH: Fellow-Citizens of the Senate, and of the House of Representatives, In meeting you at this time when the tranquility, general health and prosperity of the state afford so much cause for mutual congratulation,
observations.summary: The Gazette of the United States in Philadelphia prints the New Hampshire governor's address.
observations.note: The only printing outside New Hampshire.

newspapers.name: National Intelligencer
newspapers.title: The national intelligencer and Washington advertiser.

groups.label: Strasburgh, 17 November 1805: Vienna opens its gates
groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph dated Strasburgh, 17 November 1805, from French papers that reached New York in January 1806: 'The city of Vienna has just opened its gates for the first time to a victorious army. This glory was reserved for Frenchmen.' A report from the French side.

groups.label: Lisbon and St. Ubes: a report of a French victory
groups.definition: Printings of a report brought to Baltimore by the ship Commerce from St. Ubes, in February 1806: 'The report at Lisbon and St. Ubes was, that a recent engagement had taken place along the whole French line'. A rumour heard in Portugal at the end of December 1805, as the ship's master told it.

groups.label: The battle of Austerlitz in the papers, 1806
groups.definition: Four accounts of the battle of 2 December 1805 near Austerlitz, between the French army and the armies of Russia and Austria, as American papers printed them in February and March 1806: a notice of the British government, a letter of Marshal Berthier, the French army's thirtieth bulletin, and the Emperor's proclamation to his army. Each is one side's account. Contains those four groups.

groups.label: The London bulletin of 17 December 1805
groups.definition: Printings of a bulletin issued by the British government in London in December 1805: 'Government received last night accounts, dated at Olmutz, the 3d, by which it appears that a general battle took place on the 2d between the French and Austrian Russian armies at Wischau'. The British government's notice, on the first reports from the allied side.

groups.label: Marshal Berthier's letter to Marshal Massena on the battle
groups.definition: Printings of a letter of Marshal Berthier, the French minister of war and major general of the Grand Army, to Marshal Massena, on the battle of 2 December 1805, translated for the Baltimore American from papers brought from Leghorn: 'I am impatient, marshal, to send you' the news of the battle. The French army's own account.

groups.label: The thirtieth bulletin of the Grand Army
groups.definition: Printings of the thirtieth bulletin of the French Grand Army, dated Austerlitz, 12 Frimaire, year 14 (3 December 1805): 'The 6th Frimaire, the emperor, upon receiving the communication of the full powers of Messrs. de Stadion and de Giulay, offered previously an armistice'. The French army's official account of the battle.

groups.label: The Emperor's proclamation to the army after the battle
groups.definition: Printings of the Emperor Napoleon's proclamation to his army after the battle of 2 December 1805, dated Austerlitz, 12 Frimaire: 'Soldiers, I am satisfied with you'; an army of 100,000 men 'has been in less than four hours cut to pieces and dispersed'. A commander's address to his own army.

groups.label: The speech opening Parliament, 21 January 1806
groups.definition: Printings of the speech of the Lords Commissioners to both Houses of Parliament on 21 January 1806, made in the King's name: 'In pursuance of the authority given to us by his Majesty's Commission under the Great Seal, among other things, to declare the cause of his holding this Parliament'. It speaks of the success of the King's arms at sea and of the war on the Continent. The British government's statement. Two papers printed only a part of it, headed 'His Majesty's Message'.

groups.label: The treaty of Pressburg between Austria and France
groups.definition: Printings of the treaty of peace between Austria and France signed at Pressburg on 26 December 1805: 'His majesty the emperor of Germany and Austria, and his majesty the emperor of the French, king of Italy, equally animated with a desire to put an end to the calamities of war'. Some papers printed it with the Emperor Napoleon's act of ratification before it. A treaty.

groups.label: A Bremen letter on the sentences of the Austrian officers
groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph from London papers of February 1806: 'A private letter from Bremen of the 11th inst. contains the following article, relative to the sentences passed on the officers whose conduct produced the recent misfortunes to the House of Austria'. A report at second hand, from a private letter.

groups.label: The Emperor Napoleon's speech opening the Legislative Body, March 1806
groups.definition: Printings of the speech of the Emperor Napoleon at the opening of the French Legislative Body in March 1806: 'Since your last session, the greatest part of Europe has entered into a coalition with England. My armies have never ceased to conquer'. A head of state's own account.

groups.label: A Philadelphia report of movements in St. Domingo, May 1806
groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 10 May 1806: 'We learn from a gentleman who arrived in this city a day or two ago, from St. Domingo, that at the time of his departure there were very general movements among the subjects of the black emperor Dessalines'; the cause was not known, 'but it was said that some advices had been received by way of Jamaica'. A traveller's report at second hand, in the paper's words.

groups.label: Norfolk, May 1806: 'The French Admiral Linois taken'
groups.definition: Printings of a Norfolk paragraph of May 1806 headed 'The French Admiral Linois taken': the British frigate Tartar, arrived in Hampton Roads from Bermuda, had boarded the American ship Hunter from Lisbon, whose people had seen the French ship Marengo, 'Admiral Linois', and the frigate Belle Poule with the squadron of Sir John Borlase Warren, 'captured by Sir John'. A report passed on from ship to ship.

groups.label: Captain Dodge's report from Cape François, June 1806
groups.definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of 9 June 1806 headed 'MASSACRE AT CAPE FRANCOIS': Captain Dodge of the schooner Mary Ann, arrived from Cape François, reported 'that on the 14th and 15th of May, a general massacre of all the remaining white inhabitants of Cape Francois took place, and it was said, generally, throughout that part of this ill-fated island under the dominion of Dessalines'. A shipmaster's report, partly hearsay, in the paper's words.

groups.label: A Swedish bulletin: the Prussians cross into Lauenburg
groups.definition: Printings of a 'Swedish bulletin' from the headquarters of the Swedish army, April 1806, from London papers: reports 'received from adjutant general count Lowenhielm' said the Prussians had taken several villages near Lauenburg, and on the 23rd 'the Prussians passed the Lauenburg frontier'. One army's own account.

groups.label: Louis Napoleon proclaimed King of Holland, 1806
groups.definition: Printings of the proclamation of Louis Napoleon as King of Holland (June 1806), 'read this day to the military, and announced to the people': 'Louis Napoleon, by the Grace of God and the constitutional laws of the state, King of Holland, to all who shall see and read this, greeting'. A ruler's own proclamation.

groups.label: Francis II gives up the crown of the German Empire
groups.definition: Printings of the declaration of Francis II, emperor of Austria, giving up 'the high office of emperor of Germany', from the Paris Moniteur of 14 August 1806: 'Since the peace of Presburg all our attention and all our care have been employed to fulfil with scrupulous fidelity all the engagements' of that treaty. A ruler's own declaration.

groups.label: London, September 1806: Buenos Ayres captured
groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of September 1806: 'The official news of the capture of Buenos Ayres is received. It capitulated on the 27th of June. There fell into the hands of the English 1,291,338 dollars'. A report from the British side.

groups.label: The Hague, 17 October 1806: war between France and Prussia
groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph from Dutch papers (the Hague, 17 October 1806), translated in New York: 'Last night his excellency the Secretary of State received the important intelligence, that hostilities have commenced between the French and Prussians'. A first report of the war, through the Dutch papers.

groups.label: A shipmaster's letter from Antigua: American vessels carried in
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from the master of an American vessel, dated Antigua, 28 December 1805, first printed in the Norfolk Gazette, which had it from 'a mercantile friend': 'Every American vessel coming from a French Island, with cargo, is certain to be carried in'. One writer's account; it alleges that 'a junto consisting of the Judge, the Lawyers, the owners of privateers' shares the costs charged to Americans.

groups.label: Trade with St. Domingo: the French complaints and the act of 28 February 1806
groups.definition: The President's message to the Senate of 10 January 1806 with the French government's complaints against American trade with St. Domingo, and the act of 28 February 1806 that prohibited trade with the parts of the island 'not in possession, and under the acknowledged government of France'. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: The President's message with the French complaints on trade with St. Domingo
groups.definition: Printings of the President's message to the Senate of 10 January 1806, sending 'documents and papers ... relative to complaints by the government of France, against the commerce carried on by American citizens to the French Island of St. Domingo': letters of General Turreau, the French minister, to the Secretary of State, and of Talleyrand to General Armstrong. The complaints are the French government's own account, in its own words (Turreau writes of trade 'with the rebels of every color').

groups.label: The act of 28 February 1806 suspending trade with parts of St. Domingo
groups.definition: Printings of the act of Congress approved on 28 February 1806 'To suspend the commercial intercourse between the United States, and certain parts of the island of St. Domingo': trade with any part of the island 'not in possession, and under the acknowledged government of France, shall be, and is hereby prohibited'. A law.

groups.label: Captain Riley's journal: the Rochefort squadron at Teneriffe
groups.definition: Printings of extracts from the journal of Captain Riley of the brig Eliza and Mary, from a Nassau paper of 1 January 1806: he reached Teneriffe on 5 November 1805 and 'learnt the following intelligence': that the French squadron from Rochefort had come into Santa Cruz with prizes, and had 'sunk or burned all neutral vessels they fell in with at sea'. A shipmaster's report of what he heard.

groups.label: British seizures and impressment: papers sent to Congress, January 1806
groups.definition: Documents the President sent to Congress in January 1806 on the capture of American vessels and the impressment of American seamen by Britain: his message of 17 January, the letter of the American minister in London to Lord Mulgrave that was sent with it, and the Secretary of State's report on 'new principles interpolated into the law of nations'. Contains those three groups.

groups.label: The President's message of 17 January on British seizures and impressment
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 17 January 1806: 'In my message to both Houses of Congress, at the opening of their present session, I submitted to their attention, among other subjects, the oppression of our commerce and navigation by the irregular practices of armed vessels, public and private'. The executive's account, with documents.

groups.label: Monroe's letter to Lord Mulgrave, 23 September 1805
groups.definition: Printings of the letter of James Monroe, the American minister in London, to Lord Mulgrave of the British government, dated Great Cumberland Place, 23 September 1805, sent to Congress with the President's message of 17 January 1806: 'I flattered myself, from what passed in our last interview, that I should have been honored' with an answer. The American minister's case against the British courts' decisions on neutral trade.

groups.label: The Secretary of State's report on 'new principles' in the law of nations
groups.definition: Printings of the report of the Secretary of State to the Senate, sent with a message of the President, 'respecting "new principles interpolated into the law of nations"': 'The most important of the principles interpolated into the law of nations, is that which appears to be maintained by the British government and its prize courts'. The American government's account and argument.

groups.label: Congress and British goods, 1806
groups.definition: The House of Representatives and the President on stopping imports from Great Britain in 1806, as the papers printed it: Mr. Gregg's resolution, Mr. J. Randolph's speech against it, the National Intelligencer's paragraph on the vote for Mr. Nicholson's resolution, the act of 18 April prohibiting certain British goods, and the President's message of 3 December asking that the act be suspended. Contains those five groups.

groups.label: Mr. Gregg's resolution, 29 January
groups.definition: Printings of the resolution offered in the House by Mr. Gregg of Pennsylvania on 29 January 1806: 'Whereas Great Britain impresses citizens of the United States, and compels them to serve on board her ships of war, and also seizes and condemns vessels belonging to citizens of the United States', no goods of Great Britain or its colonies should be imported 'until equitable and satisfactory arrangements on these points shall be made'. A proposal in Congress.

groups.label: Mr. J. Randolph's speech on Mr. Gregg's resolution, 5 March
groups.definition: Printings of the report of the speech of Mr. J. Randolph of Virginia in the House on 5 March 1806, in the debate on Mr. Gregg's resolution, as the National Intelligencer gave it: 'I am extremely afraid, sir, that so far as it may depend on my acquaintance with details connected with the subject, I have very little right to address you'. A member's argument against the resolution.

groups.label: The National Intelligencer on the vote of 17 March
groups.definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 19 March 1806 on the House vote of 17 March: 'The House of Representatives, the immediate organs of the people, have, after mature deliberation, taken ground in vindication of our violated rights, on which we congratulate the nation'; with Mr. Nicholson's resolution and the yeas and nays. The Washington paper's own report and judgement.

groups.label: The act of 18 April 1806 prohibiting certain British goods
groups.definition: Printings of the act of Congress approved on 18 April 1806 'To prohibit the importation of certain goods, wares and merchandise': from 15 November 'it shall not be lawful to import into the United States, or the territories thereof, from any port or place situated in Great Britain or Ireland' the goods it lists. A law.

groups.label: The President's message of 3 December on suspending the act
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 3 December 1806: 'I have the satisfaction to inform you that the negotiation depending between the United States and the government of Great Britain is proceeding in a spirit of friendship', and that 'a temporary suspension of the act of last session, prohibiting certain importations, would, as a mark of candid disposition on our part' help it. The executive's own account and request.

groups.label: The President's message on Tunis, April 1806
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress on the dispute with Tunis, read in the House on 14 April 1806: 'During the blockade of Tripoli by the squadron of the U. S. a small cruiser, under the flag of Tunis, with two prizes' tried to enter the port. The executive's own account.

groups.label: The Leander off New York, 1806
groups.definition: Printings after a cannon shot from the British ship Leander killed an American seaman near the entrance of New York harbour on 25 April 1806, which the President's proclamation calls 'a murder': the resolutions of a meeting at New York and the President's proclamation of 3 May. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: Resolutions of a New York meeting after the Leander shot
groups.definition: Printings of the resolutions of 'a meeting of Federal Republicans' at the Tontine Coffee House, New York, in late April 1806, called 'to take into consideration the defenceless state of our harbor': 'Resolved, That the citizens of the U. S. are of right, and according to the constitution and laws of the land, entitled to the enjoyment of life, liberty, and property'. A party meeting's own resolutions.

groups.label: The President's proclamation of 3 May against the Leander, Cambrian and Driver
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 3 May 1806: Henry Whitby, commanding the British armed vessel Leander, had by a cannon shot within the waters of the United States near New York committed what it calls 'a murder'; the Leander, the Cambrian and the Driver are to leave American waters, and the President will 'forbid all intercourse with the said armed vessels' if they do not. An official document; the charge is the President's. The excerpts end before the name of the man killed.

groups.label: Fox's note to Monroe on the blockade from the Elbe to Brest
groups.definition: Printings of the note of Charles James Fox, the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, to James Monroe, the American minister (Downing Street, May 1806): the King 'has thought fit to direct that the necessary measures should be taken for the blockade of the coasts, rivers and ports from the river Elbe to the port of Brest, both inclusive'. The British government's notice.

groups.label: Hamet Caramalli's claim on the United States, 1806
groups.definition: Papers on the claim of Hamet Caramalli, 'ex-bashaw of Tripoli', on the United States after the peace with Tripoli, as the papers printed them in 1806: the President's message of 13 January, two documents sent with it (the convention Hamet made with William Eaton, and Hamet's letter to the President), and the report of the Senate committee of 17 March. Contains those four groups.

groups.label: The President's message of 13 January on Hamet Caramalli
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 13 January 1806: 'I lay before Congress the application of Hamet Caramalli, elder brother of the reigning bashaw of Tripoli, soliciting from the United States attention to his services and sufferings in the late war against that state'. The executive's own account of its dealings with him.

groups.label: The convention between William Eaton and Hamet Caramalli
groups.definition: Printings of the convention of 1805 'between the United States of America and his highness Hamet Caramalli, bashaw of Tripoli', made by William Eaton, one of the documents sent with the President's message of 13 January 1806: 'GOD IS INFINITE. ARTICLE I. There shall be a firm and perpetual peace and free intercourse' between the two. An agreement, as the message printed it.

groups.label: Hamet's letter to the President
groups.definition: Printings of a letter from Hamet ('Achmet Bashaw') to the President, sent to Congress with the message of 13 January 1806: 'For nearly eleven years, I have been labouring under the weight of misfortune'. His own account of the war against Tripoli and of his part in it with General Eaton.

groups.label: The Senate committee's report on Hamet Caramalli, 17 March
groups.definition: Printings of the report of the Senate committee on Hamet Caramalli's application, presented by Mr. Bradley on 17 March 1806. It says he was 'deceived and amused with the prospect of being placed on the throne' and proposes relief for him. A committee's findings and proposal, which differ from the President's account.

groups.label: The Spanish minister Yrujo and the government, 1806
groups.definition: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo, Spain's minister to the United States, and the American government in January 1806: his circular to the other foreign ministers against the President's message, and the letter in which the Secretary of State told him that the President expected his departure, with his answers. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: Yrujo's circular to the foreign ministers
groups.definition: Printings of the circular of the Marquis de Casa Yrujo to the foreign ministers in the United States, dated Philadelphia, 21 January 1806, in a translation from the French: 'The want of correctness which appears to prevail throughout the article, relative to Spain, of the message' of the President. With his note to the Secretary of State. The Spanish minister's own account.

groups.label: Madison's letter to Yrujo of 15 January and Yrujo's answers
groups.definition: Printings of the letter of the Secretary of State to the Marquis de Casa Yrujo of 15 January 1806: 'In consequence of the just objections which your conduct has furnished against your continuance here, as the organ of communication on the part of his Catholic Majesty', the President expects that his departure 'will not be unnecessarily postponed'; with the Marquis's answers. Each side's own words, printed by the papers with their own remarks.

groups.label: General Miranda's expedition, 1806
groups.definition: Printings about the expedition that General Francisco de Miranda fitted out at New York in the ship Leander for the coast of Caracas, as the papers printed them through 1806: questions put to the Secretary of State in February, a letter from on board the Leander in April, Miranda's proclamation of 28 June, and a report of the expedition's defeat in November. Contains those four groups.

groups.label: "Serious Questions to Mr. Madison" on General Miranda's expedition
groups.definition: Printings of a communication first printed in the Philadelphia Gazette of 19 February 1806: 'SERIOUS QUESTIONS TO MR. MADISON. Did Miranda go to Washington about the middle of December last? Had he two long interviews with you?' It asks what the government knew of the ship Leander, fitted out at New York for General Miranda's expedition. Questions that carry an allegation, by an unnamed writer.

groups.label: A letter from on board the Leander at Jacmel, 1 March
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter 'from a gentleman on board the Leander', dated Jacmel, 1 March 1806: 'General Miranda has explained to us his plan'. One member of the expedition's own account.

groups.label: General Miranda's proclamation of 28 June: 'Friends and Countrymen'
groups.definition: Printings of the proclamation that General Miranda issued on 28 June 1806 ('published at Trinidad', in one paper's words): 'FRIENDS AND COUNTRYMEN, The glorious opportunity now presents itself of relieving from oppression and arbitrary government, a people who are worthy of a better fate'. The expedition's own appeal.

groups.label: 'Miranda defeated': Captain Foster's report from Trinidad
groups.definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of November 1806 headed 'MIRANDA DEFEATED': Captain Foster, arrived from Trinidad, 'informs, that three days previous to his sailing, a Mr. Taylor, who had embarked in the expedition with Miranda, reached that place with the unpleasant intelligence of their defeat'. A report at second hand.

groups.label: The House's secret journal on Spanish affairs, published in April
groups.definition: Printings of the journal of the House of Representatives' proceedings with closed doors in December 1805 and January 1806 on the President's message of 6 December 1805 about Spain, made public at the beginning of April 1806 when 'the injunction of secrecy' was taken off: the committee's report ('The committee have beheld with just indignation the hostile spirit manifested by the court of Madrid'), the resolutions and the votes. Six papers printed the journal as the National Intelligencer gave it; three printed a shorter account with the report or the resolutions. An official record.

groups.label: General Heath declines to be Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts
groups.definition: Printings of the letter of William Heath to the Senate and House of Representatives of Massachusetts, June 1806: 'I have been notified by a very respectable committee of both Houses, that I have been elected Lieutenant Governor of the Commonwealth'; he declines the office. A public man's own statement.

groups.label: A letter from Detroit of 1 June on councils of the Indian nations
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Detroit, dated 1 June 1806: traders had reported to the acting governor 'the frequent secret councils held by the Indians', and the writer says 'We are now no longer in doubt, that the Indians are preparing to commence war against the United States'. One American writer's account of traders' reports, with his forecast.

groups.label: Spanish and American troops near the Sabine, 1806
groups.definition: Letters printed from September to November 1806 on Spanish troops east of the Sabine and the American army sent against them: a letter of 2 August headed 'HOSTILE APPEARANCE', a Natchitoches letter on Mr. Freeman's exploring party, and a letter of General Wilkinson. Each is one writer's account, from the American side. Contains those three groups.

groups.label: 'Hostile appearance': a letter of 2 August on Spanish troops
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter to the editor of a Natchez paper, dated 2 August 1806 and headed 'HOSTILE APPEARANCE': 'On or about the 18th of July ult. a detachment of Spanish troops' came toward Natchitoches. The papers give the writer's place as Natchez or Natchitoches. One writer's account.

groups.label: Natchitoches, 26 August: Mr. Freeman's party turned back
groups.definition: Printings of an extract from Natchitoches, 26 August 1806: 'Mr. Freeman returned to this place on Saturday last, after having ascended 430 miles above this place, where the Spaniards had been waiting for him'. One writer's account of the exploring party sent up the Red River.

groups.label: General Wilkinson's letter from the Rapids of Red River, 19 September
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter of General Wilkinson, dated Rapids of Red River, 19 September 1806: 'My orders, and the conduct of the Mexicans, are so much at variance'; 'I fear you will be informed blood has been spilt'. The American commander's own account, with his forecast.

groups.label: The return of Lewis and Clark, 1806
groups.definition: The first printed news of the return of Captain Lewis, Captain Clark and their party to St. Louis from the Pacific, in September 1806: the National Intelligencer's announcement and Captain Clark's letter to his brother. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: The National Intelligencer announces Captain Lewis's arrival at St. Louis
groups.definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 27 October 1806: 'It is with the sincerest pleasure, that we announce to our fellow citizens, the arrival of CAPTAIN LEWIS, with his exploring party, at St. Louis'; the President had a letter from him dated 23 September. The government paper's report.

groups.label: Captain Clark's letter to his brother, St. Louis, 23 September
groups.definition: Printings of Captain Clark's letter to his brother, dated St. Louis, 23 September 1806: 'We arrived at this place at 12 o'clock to-day, from the Pacific Ocean, where we remained during the last winter, near the entrance of the Columbia river'. One of the party's own account of the journey.

groups.label: Colonel Burr's enterprise in the papers, November 1806
groups.definition: The first widely printed items on Aaron Burr's enterprise in the West, November 1806: a Chillicothe report of an affidavit against him in Kentucky, and the President's proclamation of 27 November against a military expedition against the dominions of Spain. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: Chillicothe, 13 November: the Kentucky affidavit against Colonel Burr
groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph from the Scioto Gazette (Chillicothe, 13 November 1806) headed 'IMPORTANT COMMUNICATION': 'By a gentleman of the highest respectability from Kentucky, we are furnished with the following intelligence'; the substance of an affidavit of the United States attorney for Kentucky (printed 'Davies' or 'Daveiss') that Aaron Burr 'had formed an Association for making war against Spain, invading Mexico, and forming a distinct Empire in the Western country'. An allegation, reported at second hand.

groups.label: The President's proclamation of 27 November against a military expedition
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 27 November 1806: 'WHEREAS information has been received that sundry persons, citizens of the United States, or residents within the same are conspiring and confederating together to begin and set on foot, provide and prepare the means for a military expedition or enterprise against the dominions of Spain'; it warns citizens 'to withdraw from the same without delay'. It names no one. An official document.

groups.label: The President's annual message of 2 December 1806
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's annual message to Congress of 2 December 1806: 'It would have given me, fellow citizens, great satisfaction to announce, in the moment of your meeting, that the difficulties in our foreign relations, existing at the time of your last separation, had been amicably and justly terminated'. The executive's own account of the year.

observations.excerpt: SOLDIERS: I am satisfied with you: you have in the engagement of Austerlitz, satisfied what I expected from your intrepidity. You have decorated your eagles with an immortal glory. An army of 100,000 men, commanded by the Emperors of Russia and Austria, has been in less than four hours, cut to pieces and dispersed: those who have escaped our swords, have been drowned in the lakes.

newspapers.name: National Intelligencer
newspapers.title: The national intelligencer and Washington advertiser.

groups.label: Lübeck stormed
groups.definition: Printings of a report from Lübeck (9 or 10 November 1806) of the French attack of 6 November, which took the town from the Prussians: 'the most dreadful day in the annals of Lubeck'.

groups.label: News from Hayti by way of St. Thomas, February 1807
groups.definition: Printings of a Baltimore paragraph of 3 February 1807: from papers brought by a gentleman from St. Thomas, an account of 'operations' in 'the republic of Hayti' down to 27 December 1806, 'on which day the new Republican Constitution was adopted'. It says that General Christophe came before Port-au-Prince on 5 December with about 10,000 men 'to compel' the assembly to make him emperor, fired on General 'Pichon', the commander there, who had come out to meet him, and was driven from the town; and that news received at Jacmel on 15 January had him defeated and in flight. Six papers add, after the first sentences, the editor's promise to give the constitution 'without further loss of time than is necessary for a correct translation'. A report at second hand, from papers and news from the republic's side.

groups.label: Sir Harford Jones on the Russian army
groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of January 1807: Sir Harford Jones, back from the Russian headquarters, had never seen an army in a higher state of discipline or more eager to meet the enemy, with news of the Russian columns and of the French crossing the Vistula. It is one witness's account. Two versions circulated, dated London 6 January and 'From the Liverpool Advertiser'.

groups.label: Bennigsen's account of Pultusk
groups.definition: Printings of General Bennigsen's report to the King of Prussia on the battle of Pultusk (26 December 1806), the Russian official account, in which he writes that he repulsed the French attack on every point.

groups.label: The French army's 66th bulletin
groups.definition: Printings of the 66th bulletin of the French Grand Army (Osterode, 14 March 1807): the army rests in cantonments, with skirmishes between the outposts. New York papers had it by the brig Alonzo from Bordeaux, with the 65th.

groups.label: The 78th bulletin: the action of Spanden
groups.definition: Printings of an abstract of the 78th bulletin of the French Grand Army (Heilsberg, 12 June 1807), received at Boston from Nantes: the overtures of peace made in the winter, broken off by the Russian attacks, and the action of Spanden on 5 June.

groups.label: Armistice between France and Russia
groups.definition: Printings of the armistice between the French and Russian armies agreed at Tilsit on 21 June 1807 (signed by Berthier and Prince Labanoff), the preliminary to the peace.

groups.label: Monroe and Pinkney: a treaty agreed
groups.definition: Printings of the letter of James Monroe and William Pinkney from London, 27 December 1806, to the Secretary of State: they had agreed with the British commissioners to conclude a treaty on all the points of their negotiation, on terms they trusted the government would approve. The President sent it to Congress on 19 February 1807. Several papers printed it again in October and November, after the treaty had been set aside.

groups.label: The Driver at Charleston
groups.definition: Reports of the British sloop of war Driver, which the President had barred from American ports, anchoring in Charleston harbour in April and May 1807: the commandant of Fort Johnson's demand that she leave, and her commander's answer. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: Fort Johnson orders the Driver out
groups.definition: Printings of the letter of Captain Michael Kalteisen, commandant of Fort Johnson in Charleston harbour (2 May 1807), to the commander of the British sloop of war Driver, which a proclamation of the President had barred from American harbours: she must leave within twenty-four hours. Most papers printed it inside a Charleston report of the Driver's arrival, reprinted from New York; the papers give the proclamation different dates.

groups.label: The Driver's commander answers
groups.definition: Printings of the answer of Captain William Love, commanding the British sloop of war Driver (Rebellion Roads, Charleston, 3 May 1807), to Captain Kalteisen: he doubted the authority by which the demand was written, knew nothing of a proclamation of May 1807, and would not leave until ready.

groups.label: The Chesapeake affair
groups.definition: Documents and reports of the attack of the British ship Leopard on the American frigate Chesapeake off the Virginia capes on 22 June 1807, and its aftermath, as the 1807 papers printed them: the National Intelligencer's account, the President's proclamation of 2 July, Admiral Berkeley's order, the opinion of the court of inquiry on Commodore Barron, and the House committee's report. Contains those five groups; the wider coverage is not included.

groups.label: The National Intelligencer's account of the attack
groups.definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's account of 26 June 1807, headed 'British Outrage': the Leopard, one of the British squadron at the capes, followed the Chesapeake out to sea, demanded three men said to be deserters, and fired on her until she struck.

groups.label: The President's proclamation of 2 July
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 2 July 1807, which recited the attack on the Chesapeake and required all armed vessels bearing commissions under the British government to leave the harbours and waters of the United States, forbidding all intercourse with them.

groups.label: Admiral Berkeley's order
groups.definition: Printings of the order of Vice-Admiral George Cranfield Berkeley, British commander in chief at Halifax (1 June 1807), directing the captains under his command, if they met the Chesapeake at sea, to show her captain the order and search her for the deserters named in its margin. American papers printed it from late July.

groups.label: The court of inquiry on the Chesapeake
groups.definition: Printings of the opinion of the naval court of inquiry held on board the Chesapeake at Norfolk (5 October to 4 November 1807) on the conduct of Commodore James Barron: among other findings, that the Chesapeake was prematurely surrendered when she was nearly prepared for battle. Includes one printing of its conclusion only.

groups.label: The House committee's report
groups.definition: Printings of a summary of the report made to the House on 17 November 1807 by Mr. Blount for the committee on the part of the President's message relating to aggressions, with the report's conclusion quoted: the outrage on the Chesapeake 'has been stamped with circumstances of indignity and insult' with scarcely a parallel.

groups.label: Commodore Douglas and the Mayor of Norfolk
groups.definition: The letters exchanged in July 1807 between Commodore John E. Douglas, commanding the British squadron in Hampton Roads, and Richard E. Lee, Mayor of Norfolk, over the Norfolk committee's ban on communication with the British ships, with the report of Littleton W. Tazewell, who carried the Mayor's answer. Contains those four groups.

groups.label: Commodore Douglas's letter of 3 July
groups.definition: Printings of Commodore Douglas's letter to the Mayor of Norfolk (Bellona, Hampton Roads, 3 July 1807): unless the committee's resolution forbidding communication with the British consul and ships was annulled, he would stop every vessel bound in or out of Norfolk; it rested with the inhabitants 'either to engage in a war or remain on terms of peace'.

groups.label: The Mayor's answer of 4 July
groups.definition: Printings of the answer of Richard E. Lee, Mayor of Norfolk, to Commodore Douglas (4 July 1807): 'the American people are not to be intimidated by menace'; the ban was an act of individuals, not of the government, and the inhabitants would protect themselves against any aggression.

groups.label: Tazewell's report to the Mayor
groups.definition: Printings of the report of Littleton W. Tazewell to the Mayor of Norfolk (5 July 1807) on delivering the Mayor's answer on board the Bellona: Douglas said his letter had been misapprehended and that he intended no menace. Includes one shorter account of the report.

groups.label: Commodore Douglas's letter of 6 July
groups.definition: Printings of Commodore Douglas's second letter to the Mayor of Norfolk (Bellona, Hampton Roads, 6 July 1807): every circumstance had been discussed with the gentlemen who carried the Mayor's answer, and he would use every exertion, consistent with the honour of the British flag, toward an amicable end.

groups.label: Robert MacDonald's funeral at Norfolk, June 1807
groups.definition: Printings of a Norfolk paragraph of 29 June 1807: Robert MacDonald, 'one of the seamen wounded on board the Chesapeake frigate', died at the Marine Hospital, and his funeral the day before was 'attended by nearly four thousand citizens', with a procession of boats, minute guns, colours at half mast and a sermon at Christ Church; the paper prints the order of the procession. A local report of a public funeral.

groups.label: The National Intelligencer on the seamen the Leopard sought
groups.definition: Printings of a Washington paragraph of 29 July 1807 from the National Intelligencer: 'Much error having appeared in the accounts circulated' of what passed between the government and the British minister, Erskine, 'in the case of the seamen, to obtain whom the Leopard made the late attack on the Chesapeake', it states that his application for their surrender was refused, that naval commanders had orders not to recruit British deserters, and that the government had reason to believe the seamen were native citizens of the United States. The National Intelligencer's own account; it adds a note with the seamen's names and particulars as Captain Barron reported them.

groups.label: An Antwerp letter: ships to or from England to be taken
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a house in Antwerp to one in Bordeaux (28 September 1807), brought by the Sally-Barker-Windsor: 'We understand' that the Emperor had ordered every vessel bound to or from England to be captured, 'a mortal blow to the American commerce'. It reports a rumoured order.

groups.label: London: 'the question of peace or war'
groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of October 1807: the British ministers had delivered to Monroe and Pinkney their final answer on the leading points in dispute, so that 'the question of peace or war with America' was decided as far as it could be in England, and Monroe was preparing to leave. It is a London paper's report and forecast.

groups.label: General Wilkinson's speech in the court at New Orleans
groups.definition: Printings of General Wilkinson's address to the court at New Orleans, as a letter from that city of 18 December 1806 reports it (Washington, 21 January 1807): appearing on a writ of habeas corpus for a man he had arrested, he said he was 'called to account for an act in which I glory', warned that 'the artifices of the confederates' must no longer 'cheat the public judgment' and that 'treason stalks abroad', and spoke of 'the friends of Burr and rebellion'. The report adds that he then charged two lawyers with being parties to the conspiracy. The general's own words, as the letter gives them.

groups.label: Burr's conspiracy and trial
groups.definition: Documents and reports of Aaron Burr's alleged conspiracy and his trial, as the 1807 papers printed them: the President's message to Congress of 22 January, a New York report of news from New Orleans (February), Chief Justice Marshall's opinion on committing Burr (April), the jury's verdict in the treason trial (September), and Marshall's opinion of 20 October after the trial. Contains those five groups; the wider coverage is not included. The message and the reports carry allegations; the jury found the charge of treason not proved.

groups.label: The President's message on the conspiracy
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 22 January 1807, sent at the request of the House, on 'an illegal combination of private individuals' against the peace of the Union and a military expedition planned against Spanish territory, with the measures taken to suppress it. It names Aaron Burr as the principal actor. Its enclosures (General Wilkinson's affidavit and letters) are not counted separately.

groups.label: News from New Orleans: 'Burr in arms'
groups.definition: Printings of a New York report (3 February 1807) of news from New Orleans brought by the brig Neptune: General Wilkinson had refused Burr passage, the city was under arms, and Burr was said to be at Natchez with 600 men and an advanced guard of 200 cavalry. The numbers are a report, not an observed fact.

groups.label: Marshall's opinion on committing Burr
groups.definition: Printings of Chief Justice Marshall's opinion of 1 April 1807 at Richmond on the motion to commit Aaron Burr on two charges: he committed him for setting on foot an expedition against Spanish territory, a misdemeanor, but not for treason, finding no proof yet that war had been levied. Includes one printing of a summary of the opinion.

groups.label: The verdict: 'not proved to be guilty'
groups.definition: Printings of the jury's written verdict in Aaron Burr's trial for treason at Richmond on 1 September 1807, 'We of the jury find that Aaron Burr is not proved to be guilty under this indictment by any evidence submitted to us. We therefore find him not guilty', quoted in accounts of that day's proceedings, with Burr's objection to its form. Three different accounts carry it; most papers printed the same one.

groups.label: Marshall's opinion of 20 October
groups.definition: Printings of Chief Justice Marshall's opinion of 20 October 1807 at Richmond, after the treason trial, on the motion to commit Burr, Blennerhassett and Israel Smith to be tried elsewhere for treason and misdemeanor: he held it improper to commit them on the charge of treason, and committed Burr and Blennerhassett for preparing and providing the means for a military expedition. Includes printings of a Richmond report that quotes the opinion's conclusion.

groups.label: Congress called early, 1807
groups.definition: The President's proclamation of 30 July 1807 calling Congress to meet on 26 October instead of in December, and his message to the session on 27 October. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: The proclamation calling Congress
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 30 July 1807 that 'great and weighty matters' required Congress to meet at Washington on Monday 26 October. The National Intelligencer printed it seven times, as a standing notice.

groups.label: The President's message of 27 October
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress at the opening of the special session, 27 October 1807: the British answer on the treaty, the attack on the Chesapeake and the proclamation that followed, the defence of the ports, the Burr trials, the finances, and the Indian nations.

newspapers.name: National Intelligencer
newspapers.title: The national intelligencer and Washington advertiser.

groups.label: Lisbon under the French, December 1807
groups.definition: Printings of news from Lisbon papers of December 1807, brought by the brig Perseverance: decrees of the French general in chief after the occupation, forbidding the use of arms to all but the military, confiscating English property and making French and Spanish money current.

groups.label: Revolution in Spain: two letters from Alicante
groups.definition: Two letters from Alicante, both dated 27 March 1808, on the rising at Aranjuez and the fall of the Prince of Peace, as American papers printed them in May 1808, several of them side by side ('Extract of another Letter'). Contains those two groups. Each is one letter-writer's account.

groups.label: Alicante letter: 'a rumour being spread at Aranjuez'
groups.definition: Printings of a letter from Alicante of 27 March 1808, received at Boston and introduced as 'interesting particulars of the affairs of Spain': a rumour that the royal family meant to leave for Cadiz and embark on the English squadron brought crowds to the palace at Aranjuez; the Prince of Peace fell, and the King resigned his crown to his son. One paper prints only its later part.

groups.label: Alicante letter: the guards ordered to Aranjuez
groups.definition: Printings of another letter from Alicante of 27 March 1808, which reached Boston by the brig Sally: on the evening of 18 March the Prince of Peace ordered the Spanish and Walloon guards to Aranjuez; a report that the royal family meant to flee to Gibraltar and America brought a crowd to the palace crying 'kill the traitor'.

groups.label: Charles IV names Murat lieutenant-general of Spain
groups.definition: Printings of Charles IV's letter to Murat, 'Brother, my absence and infirmities…', enclosing the royal decree (Bayonne, 4 May 1808) that made him lieutenant-general of the kingdom, to govern in the King's name. A document issued under French control.

groups.label: Governor Sevier's letter from Marble Springs, May 1808
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter of Governor Sevier of Tennessee to a friend at Staunton, Virginia, dated Marble Springs, 14 May 1808, first printed in the Staunton Eagle: an express from General Jackson had reported that '440 Creeks and 12 whites' had taken a position on the south bank of the Tennessee near the mouth of Duck river and had killed about twenty persons; 'If this be true we shall have warm work this summer'. The Eagle adds that two companies of West Tennessee militia were on duty on the frontier. A report at second hand, which the governor passes on with a condition.

groups.label: The British order in council of 4 July: peace with Spain
groups.definition: Printings of the order of the King in Council of 4 July 1808: in view of the Spanish nation's 'glorious exertions' against France, all hostilities against Spain were to cease, the blockade of Spanish ports not held by France was raised, and Spanish vessels were admitted to British ports.

groups.label: News from Spain by the Arcturus
groups.definition: Printings of a Boston Gazette report of 5 September 1808: the ship Arcturus, 48 days from St. Sebastian, had arrived with P. R. Livingston, bearer of dispatches from the French government, and with passengers' accounts that General Dupont had been defeated at Cordova and Andujar. A report from passengers ('is said').

groups.label: General Reding's dispatch on the battle of Baylen
groups.definition: Printings of the dispatch of the Spanish general Reding to General Castaños, 22 July 1808, on the action of 19 July near Baylen, in which Dupont attacked the Spanish camp; printed from Spanish papers. One army's own account.

groups.label: The conventions in Portugal, 1808
groups.definition: The two conventions of late August and early September 1808 that ended the French occupation of Portugal, as American papers printed them from London papers in October and November: the surrender of the Russian fleet in the Tagus, and the evacuation of Portugal by the French army. Contains those two groups.

groups.label: The convention for the Russian fleet in the Tagus
groups.definition: Printings of the articles agreed on 3 September 1808 between the Russian Vice-Admiral Seniavin and Admiral Sir Charles Cotton for the surrender of the Russian fleet in the Tagus, to be held by Britain until after a peace, with Cotton's covering letter.

groups.label: The convention for the evacuation of Portugal
groups.definition: Printings of the definitive convention of 30 August 1808 (the Convention of Cintra) between the British and French commanders in Portugal: the French army was to leave Portugal and be carried to France in British ships.

groups.label: Orders and decrees against neutral trade
groups.definition: Three measures of the warring powers against neutral commerce, as American papers printed them in the first half of 1808: the British Order in Council of 11 November 1807, a merchant house's account of Napoleon's Milan decree, and the British instructions of 11 April 1808 on provisions for the West Indies. Contains those three groups; the grouping is by subject.

groups.label: The British Order in Council of 11 November 1807
groups.definition: Printings of the order of the King in Council of 11 November 1807 that put the ports of France and her allies, and every port from which the British flag was excluded, under the restrictions of a blockade, as retaliation for the French decrees.

groups.label: An Amsterdam letter on the Milan decree
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Daniel Crommelin and Sons, Amsterdam, 30 December 1807, received at New York on 13 February 1808: official news of a decree of the French Emperor at Milan under which vessels that had submitted to British search or paid duties in Britain were to be treated as denationalised. It is a merchant house's summary, not the decree.

groups.label: British instructions of 11 April on provisions for the colonies
groups.definition: Printings of the King's instructions to the commanders of British ships of war and privateers (Windsor, 11 April 1808): they were not to interrupt neutral vessels laden with lumber and provisions bound to the British colonies, under the conditions the instructions set.

groups.label: Algiers and the American ships, 1808
groups.definition: A New Bedford report of February 1808 that Algiers had declared war on the United States, the American consul general's circular of the same weeks that the dispute was settled, and a June report of the Dey's new demands. Contains those three groups.

groups.label: New Bedford: 'War with Algiers'
groups.definition: Printings of a New Bedford handbill of 30 January 1808: the ship Honestus, 42 days from the Downs, had been told off Cape Trafalgar that Algiers had declared war against America and captured American vessels. It is a report; the consul general's circular, printed in the same weeks, says the dispute had been settled.

groups.label: Lear's circular: peace with Algiers
groups.definition: Printings of the circular of Tobias Lear, American consul general at Algiers (16 December 1807), received at Salem in February 1808: three American vessels detained by an Algerine frigate, because the annuities were two years in arrears, had been released after he settled with the Dey.

groups.label: Washington: the Dey of Algiers makes new demands
groups.definition: Printings of a National Intelligencer paragraph of 24 June 1808 ('We understand'): after the settlement of December, the Dey had demanded in March two thousand dollars a man for Algerine seamen lost in the rescue of a captured American vessel, threatening to put Consul Lear in chains. It is a report from the government's paper.

groups.label: The British and French papers laid before Congress, 1808
groups.definition: The President's message of 22 March 1808 and the correspondence with Britain and France it laid before Congress, as the papers printed it from March to May: Canning and Monroe on the Chesapeake (No. II), the letters of George Rose and James Madison on Rose's mission (No. III), and Champagny's letter to Armstrong of 15 January, made public on 2 April. Contains those four groups.

groups.label: The President's message of 22 March
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message of 22 March 1808 laying before Congress the correspondence with Britain on the Chesapeake, the unratified treaty and Rose's mission, and with France.

groups.label: Canning and Monroe on the Chesapeake
groups.definition: Printings of the correspondence between George Canning and James Monroe on the attack on the Chesapeake, with Monroe's letters to the Secretary of State (No. II of the papers laid before Congress), counted by its first document, Canning's note of 25 July 1807 on the first news of the attack.

groups.label: Rose and Madison on Rose's mission
groups.definition: Printings of the correspondence between George Rose, the British envoy, and James Madison, Secretary of State (No. III of the papers laid before Congress), counted by its first letter: Rose's of 26 January 1808, that his instructions forbade any negotiation while the President's proclamation of 2 July 1807 remained in force; with Madison's answer of 5 March and Rose's reply of 17 March.

groups.label: Champagny to Armstrong, 15 January 1808
groups.definition: Printings of the letter of the French foreign minister, Champagny, to General Armstrong, the American minister (Paris, 15 January 1808), made public by Congress on 2 April: the Emperor considered war as existing between England and the United States from the day England published her decrees, and had 'no doubt of a declaration of war against her by the United States'. It is France's own document.

groups.label: Canning in the Commons on America, 24 June
groups.definition: Printings of a report of George Canning's remarks in the House of Commons on 24 June 1808, answering Mr. Whitbread: no communication had come from the American government since Mr. Rose's return; he could only conjecture that America was negotiating with France; reparation for the Chesapeake had been offered without giving up the right of search. The papers' heading calls him the Prime Minister; he was Foreign Secretary.

groups.label: The embargo laws
groups.definition: The Embargo Act of 22 December 1807 and the acts of the first session of the Tenth Congress that extended it, enforced it and allowed the President to suspend it, as the 1808 papers printed them, most of them 'by authority': the supplementary act of 9 January, the additional act of 12 March, the act of 22 April authorising a suspension and the act of 25 April. Contains those five groups. Only 1808 printings are included; the Embargo Act was first printed in December 1807.

groups.label: The Embargo Act of 22 December 1807
groups.definition: Printings of the act of 22 December 1807 laying an embargo on all ships and vessels in the ports and harbors of the United States: no clearance for a foreign port, and bonds for coasting vessels. This group holds the act's 1808 printings; it was first printed in late December 1807, and those printings are not included.

groups.label: The supplementary act of 9 January
groups.definition: Printings of the act of 9 January 1808 supplementary to the Embargo Act: vessels licensed for the coasting trade, and fishing and whaling vessels, may not depart without bond that they will not go to a foreign port, with penalties for evading the embargo.

groups.label: The additional act of 12 March
groups.definition: Printings of the act of 12 March 1808 in addition to the supplementary act: no boat that is neither registered nor licensed, and no foreign vessel, may depart, and goods may not be exported from the United States by land or by water.

groups.label: The act allowing the President to suspend the embargo
groups.definition: Printings of the act of 22 April 1808 authorising the President, during the recess of Congress, to suspend the embargo in whole or in part if peace, a suspension of hostilities or changes in the belligerents' measures made American commerce sufficiently safe.

groups.label: The act of 25 April enforcing the embargo
groups.definition: Printings of the act of 25 April 1808 in addition to the embargo acts: vessels whose trade is confined to bays, sounds, rivers and lakes must give bond, and collectors may detain vessels and unusual deposits of goods suspected of evading the embargo.

groups.label: Charges against General Wilkinson, 1808
groups.definition: Documents and reports of the charges that General James Wilkinson had taken money from the Spanish government, as the 1808 papers printed them: his challenge to John Randolph and Randolph's answer (December 1807), Daniel Clark's statement to the House, the President's message of 20 January, and the opinion of the military court of inquiry (printed from 4 July). Contains those four groups. The statement and the letters are allegations and each writer's own account; the court found no evidence.

groups.label: Wilkinson's challenge and Randolph's answer
groups.definition: Printings of two letters of 24 and 25 December 1807, from a pamphlet: General James Wilkinson asks John Randolph, a member of the House, for satisfaction for words injurious to his reputation, and Randolph refuses. Each letter is its writer's own account.

groups.label: Daniel Clark's statement to the House
groups.definition: Printings of the statement of Daniel Clark, delegate from the Territory of Orleans, laid before the House on 11 January 1808 and sworn before Judge Cranch: that General Wilkinson had dealings with the Spanish government and received money from it. It is an allegation.

groups.label: The President's message of 20 January on Wilkinson
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to the House of 20 January 1808, answering its resolutions of 13 January on General Wilkinson: a court of inquiry, asked for by Wilkinson, was already sitting, and he reported what the executive's records held on foreign intrigues and on any corrupt receipt of money by an officer of the United States.

groups.label: The court of inquiry's opinion on Wilkinson
groups.definition: Printings of the opinion of the military court of inquiry at Washington on General Wilkinson (signed by its president, Colonel Burbeck, and approved by the President), printed from 4 July 1808: it found no evidence that Wilkinson had received a pension or money from the Spanish government for corrupt purposes.

groups.label: The President's message on more troops, February 1808
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of February 1808 (communicated on 26 February) recommending an increase of the military force, regular and volunteer, with the Secretary of War's letter proposing new regiments; the message and the letter are one publication, counted once.

groups.label: The embargo at home, spring 1808
groups.definition: Reports and executive documents on the embargo's working in April and May 1808: a Georgia letter on its effect at Mobile and Pensacola, the President's proclamation on Lake Champlain, and his letter to five governors on supplies of flour. Contains those three groups; the grouping is by subject.

groups.label: A Georgia letter: Mobile and Pensacola
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman in Georgia (14 March 1808): the embargo had left the citizens of Mobile and Pensacola 'almost in a state of starvation', with the prices of corn and flour there. It is one unnamed correspondent's report.

groups.label: The President's proclamation on Lake Champlain
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 19 April 1808: persons on Lake Champlain and the adjacent country were combining to obstruct the embargo laws, too strong for the ordinary course of justice, and were commanded to disperse. It alleges insurrection; several papers printed it from the Rutland Herald of 30 April.

groups.label: The President's letter to the governors on flour
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's letter of 6 May 1808 to the governors of Orleans, Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts and New Hampshire: since shipments of flour had become generally suspicious, the governors might certify merchants they trusted to bring in flour for the needs of their states.

groups.label: John Quincy Adams resigns from the Senate
groups.definition: Printings of John Quincy Adams's letter of 8 June 1808 to the Massachusetts legislature, resigning his seat in the Senate after the legislature had passed resolutions disapproving of measures he had supported.

groups.label: Jefferson's answer to the New Hampshire legislature
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's answer to the address of the New Hampshire legislature of 14 June 1808, which had approved the measures of his administration, the embargo among them.

groups.label: Jefferson's answer to the petitions against the embargo
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's answer to the petition of the Boston town meeting, which had asked him to suspend the embargo: he could not suspend it while the belligerents' edicts stood, and only the legislature could prescribe its course. The Portland Gazette prints the same text as the answer to Portland's petition.

groups.label: 'Melancholy Event': Burlington, Vermont, August 1808
groups.definition: Printings of a Burlington (Vermont) paragraph of 5 August 1808, headed 'Melancholy Event': a revenue cutter with a lieutenant, a sergeant and twelve privates, sent by the collector of the customs after a large boat 'well known to have been some time employed in smuggling', took her on Onion river; men on the bank then fired on the cutter's crew, and two of the crew and a man of the town were killed. The report says that eight persons were taken and put in gaol, that a jury of inquest found 'wilful murder', and that 'all opinion' should be suspended until the facts were known. A local report.

groups.label: General Wilkinson's challenge to Robert Goodloe Harper, October 1808
groups.definition: Printings of notes exchanged at Baltimore on 26 and 27 October 1808, as published there: General James Wilkinson's note to Captain Robert Goodloe Harper, commanding a company of volunteer artillery, charging that Harper had 'secretly assailed the General's honour' and demanding 'the only admissible atonement'; Harper's refusal, which says that his advice to Mr. Clark to lay before Congress documents on Wilkinson's 'connection with the Spanish government' gave no ground for a challenge; and Wilkinson's reply. Each man's own words. The papers print them under their own introductions or headings, such as 'MODERN CHIVALRY' and '"HECTOR" AGAIN.'

groups.label: The President's message of 8 November and its documents
groups.definition: President Jefferson's last annual message, at the opening of the second session of the Tenth Congress on 8 November 1808, and three of the diplomatic papers sent with it, which the papers printed in later issues and in instalments: Canning's note to Pinkney, an extract of Armstrong's letter from France, and Madison's letter to Erskine. Contains those four groups.

groups.label: The President's message of 8 November
groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's annual message to Congress of 8 November 1808: the overtures to Britain and France had failed, their edicts stood, and Congress was to decide what course to take on the embargo.

groups.label: Canning's answer to Pinkney, 23 September
groups.definition: Printings of George Canning's note to William Pinkney (Foreign Office, 23 September 1808), sent to Congress with the President's message: Britain declined the American offer to suspend the embargo as to Britain if the Orders in Council were withdrawn. The British side's own statement.

groups.label: Armstrong to Madison, 28 August
groups.definition: Printings of an extract of General Armstrong's letter to the Secretary of State from Bourbon l'Archambault, 28 August 1808, sent to Congress with the President's message: he would not return to Paris to renew his discussions with Champagny, being convinced that a new attempt would be useless and probably injurious.

groups.label: Madison to Erskine on the Orders in Council, 25 March
groups.definition: Printings of the Secretary of State's letter to David Erskine, the British minister (25 March 1808), sent to Congress with the President's message: the Orders in Council of November 1807 could not be justified as retaliation for the French decrees.

groups.label: The House committee's report on foreign relations
groups.definition: Printings of the report in part of the House committee on the part of the President's message concerning foreign relations (presented on 22 November 1808 by George W. Campbell): the choice lay between submission, war with both Britain and France, and continuing the embargo with stricter enforcement; with three resolutions.

observations.excerpt: LATEST FROM PORTUGAL. By the brig Perseverance, capt. Atkins, arrived at the Vineyard, from Lisbon, papers are received to the 13th Dec.—The following are some extracts:— LISBON, DEC. 8.—The use of arms, excepting by the military, is this day prohibited, under severe penalties. It is also decreed this day, that English property, of every kind, shall be confiscated;
observations.summary: News from Lisbon by the brig Perseverance: under the French general, the use of arms is forbidden and English property confiscated (December 1807).
observations.note: Earliest printing found. Prints its own introduction ('papers are received to the 13th Dec.') and begins the extracts at 8 December.

observations.excerpt: BOSTON, February 22. LATEST FROM PORTUGAL. By the arrival, at the Vineyard, of the brig Perseverance , captain Atkins, we have received a file of Lisbon papers to the 19th December. Excepting sundry decrees of Juan, the general in chief of the French army, stationed there, they contain no news of any interest whatever. LISBON, December 4.
